sources.news_title: U.S. Jobs Surge: 165K Added, Unemployment Drops to 4.1%
sources.text:
The U.S. economy added 165,000 jobs in October and unemployment fell to 4.1 percent, more than double what economists had forecast.
Private employers did the heavy lifting. Hiring beat expectations across factories and services, earlier months were revised higher, and more Americans stepped into the labor force.
Breitbart reported that economists surveyed by Econoday had looked for only 62,000 new jobs and an unemployment rate stuck at 4.2 percent. The October print cleared that bar by a wide margin.
Private payrolls rose by 159,000. Forecasters had expected 59,000. Manufacturing, which many thought would be flat, added 19,000 positions on its own.
The headline gain was not a one-month blip. August’s estimate was revised up by 53,000, from 133,000 to 186,000. September’s figure moved up by 31,000, from 29,000 to 60,000.
Taken together, those changes mean payrolls were 84,000 higher than earlier reports had shown. The prior month’s private-payroll estimate was lifted from a gain of 46,000 to 78,000.
That pattern matters for anyone tracking the real trend, not a single print. Soft first estimates gave way to firmer numbers once fuller data arrived.
Manufacturing payrolls rose by 19,000 in October. Economists surveyed by Econoday had expected zero growth there.
Durable-goods plants led the way with 25,000 jobs. Nondurable payrolls fell by 6,000. Automakers added 4,100 jobs. Computer and electronic product manufacturing grew by 7,000. Machinery and primary metals each added 4,000.
September’s manufacturing gain was revised from 6,000 to 13,000. Since December, manufacturing has added 101,000 jobs.
The services sector added 144,000 jobs. Professional and business services accounted for 70,000 of them. Healthcare and social assistance added 55,100. Transportation and warehousing added 24,800. Finance added 7,000. Retailers added 6,000.
Not every corner expanded. Wholesale jobs dipped by 9,100. Information payrolls contracted by 1,000.
Federal government employment shrank by 1,000. Excluding the postal service, federal employment fell by 5,000.
State government employment expanded by 8,000, driven by a 11,500 rise in state education jobs while other state employment fell. Local government employment declined by 1,000.
In short, the October surge was a private-sector story. Taxpayers did not underwrite the beat.
Average hourly earnings rose 0.4 percent in October. The prior month’s increase was 0.3 percent and had already come in above the top of estimates. That earlier wage gain was revised up from 0.1 percent to 0.3 percent.
Compared with a year ago, average hourly earnings are up 3.1 percent. The average workweek held steady at 34.4 hours.
Labor force participation edged up from 61.8 percent to 61.9 percent. Unemployment fell even as more people entered the job hunt, a sign of demand strong enough to pull workers in, not a mirage created by people quitting the search.
Many economists now put the “break-even” rate of job growth, the pace needed just to keep unemployment steady, as low as zero. Others peg it between 10,000 and 55,000 jobs a month.
That is a sharp change from the recent past. When immigration ran at higher levels from 2021 through 2024, the economy needed to add more than 100,000 jobs every month just to keep up with labor-force growth.
October’s 165,000 gain sits far above those lower break-even ranges. It also tops the old, higher threshold from the high-inflow years. Baby Boom retirements continue in the background, which is one reason the bar for “enough” hiring has shifted.
Markets are already looking ahead. Investors are trying to judge whether the Federal Reserve will raise its benchmark interest rate for a second time when policymakers meet next month.
A hot jobs print with rising wages and higher participation gives the Fed more to weigh. Growth this far above forecast is harder to dismiss as noise, especially after upward revisions to August and September.
Still, the report’s core message is straightforward. Hiring was broad, private employers led, factories surprised to the upside, and the jobless rate moved down while participation moved up.
Strong private payrolls, firmer wages, and a lower unemployment rate are what a healthy labor market is supposed to look like, and October delivered the beat in black and white.

U.S. adds 165,000 jobs as unemployment rate falls to 4.1%
WASHINGTON >> U.S. job growth accelerated in October and the unemployment rate fell to 4.1%, suggesting that the labor market could be strengthening after stumbling in mid-summer and keeping the Federal Reserve on track to raise interest rates in December.
The Labor Department’s closely watched employment report today also showed the economy added 84,000 more jobs in August and September than previously reported. The decline in the unemployment rate from 4.2% in September was despite more people piling into the labor force, likely seeking to cushion themselves against higher living costs resulting from the conflict in the Middle East.
The better-than-expected report followed on the heels of data this week showing a rise in job openings in September, which combined with historically low layoffs has raised the specter of the labor market tightening.
“The labor market is heating up across-the-board and supports our view that the Fed will raise the policy rate again in December,” said Kathy Bostjancic, chief economist at Nationwide.
Nonfarm payrolls jumped by 165,000 jobs last month after an upwardly revised 60,000 gain in September, the Labor Department’s Bureau of Labor Statistics said. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast payrolls advancing 65,000 after a previously reported 29,000 increase in September.
Estimates ranged from 35,000 to 125,000 jobs. August’s employment gains were revised up to 186,000 from the previously estimated 133,000. Employment growth averaged 137,000 over the last three months compared to an average loss of 45,000 during the same period in 2025. Some economists were skeptical of the labor market’s newfound strength.

“Recent improvements in the employment situation largely relate to a major jump in federal government spending in the third quarter, as well as an unprecedented surge in election spending reported to be near $12 billion within a relatively short time frame of August to October,” said Brian Bethune, an economics professor at Boston College.
Last month’s broad-based increase in payrolls was led by the professional and business services industry, which added 70,000 jobs, well above the average monthly gain of 15,000 over the past 12 months. Those jobs were in professional, scientific and technical services as well as administrative and support, waste management and remediation services.
Healthcare employment increased by 42,000 jobs, mostly at hospitals and home healthcare services. The transportation and warehousing sector added 25,000 positions, the majority of them couriers and messengers, consistent with strong domestic demand.
Manufacturing payrolls rose by 19,000 jobs, spread across computer and electronic products, machinery and primary metals. The increases are likely linked to the artificial intelligence buildout. There were modest job gains in the retail, financial activities and government sectors.
Construction shed 3,000 jobs, the bulk of them residential specialty trade contractors. Residential building construction employment also declined against the backdrop of high mortgage rates, which have depressed homebuilding. Home renovations have also been trending down.
Leisure and hospitality employment dropped by 13,000 positions, concentrated in the accommodation and food services sector. The share of industries reporting growth last month increased to 57.6% from 54.2% in September. The average workweek was unchanged at 34.4 hours.
Financial markets priced in a roughly 80% chance of a rate hike at the U.S. central bank’s meeting next month, up from 66.9% on Thursday, CME’s FedWatch tool showed.
The Fed last week left its benchmark overnight interest rate in the 3.75%-4.00% range. Next Tuesday’s consumer inflation report for October could offer more clues on the course of monetary policy in early 2027. Economists are also watching the stock market after a tech-sector rout on Thursday amid fears a Democratic-led Congress could lead to tougher AI regulation.
Stocks on Wall Street were trading higher. The dollar gained versus a basket of currencies. U.S. Treasury yields rose.
Economists estimated the economy needs to create at least 40,000 jobs per month to keep up with growth in the working-age population. The so-called breakeven rate has declined from roughly 150,000 in 2024 because of the smaller labor force as the Trump administration cracks down on immigration.
Household employment, a volatile measure, increased 463,000 in October, outpacing the 421,000 people who entered the labor force. About 1.589 million people have joined the labor force over the past three months, lifting the participation rate to 61.9% from 61.6% in August. But many of them, mostly re-entrees, have not found work.
Young adults have virtually been locked out of the labor market, with AI eliminating some entry-level positions.
The median duration of unemployment jumped to 11.9 weeks, the longest since November 2021, from 11.5 weeks in September. There were more people working part-time for economic reasons last month, with the number increasing 339,000 to 4.840 million.
A broader measure of unemployment, which includes people who want to work but have given up searching and those working part-time because they cannot find full-time employment, rose to 7.9% from 7.6% in September. Historically low layoffs have anchored the labor market.
Though hiring is picking up, it has lagged economic growth, with gross domestic product increasing at a 3.4% annualized rate in the third quarter. Economists said uncertainty from the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran as well as the impact of AI on staffing needs had left businesses hesitant to increase head count.
“More than a quarter of unemployed workers were searching for six months or longer in October, a share rarely seen outside the aftermath of a recession,” said Cory Stahle, senior economist at the Indeed Hiring Lab. “And even when employers do hire, job posting data suggests that they have increasingly tilted their hiring toward experience, leaving people early in their careers with even fewer ways in.”
Wage growth maintained its moderate pace, increasing 3.1% in the 12 months through October after advancing 3.2% in September. While that underscored the disinflationary impulse from the labor market, it illustrated the continued erosion of household incomes. Consumer prices rose 3.7% year-on-year in September.
Anger over inflation resulted in President Donald Trump’s Republican Party losing control of Congress to Democrats in Tuesday’s midterm elections.
“The American public will continue to skeptically look at the current economic expansion which is highly skewed towards upper- end households and corporates that are profiting from strong underlying demand and robust non-residential investment,” said Joseph Brusuelas, chief economist at RSM.

sources.news_title: ‘Employers are still cautious’: Jobs gains were more ‘treat’ than ‘trick’ in October * WorldNetDaily * by Jack McGeever, Daily Caller News Foundation
sources.text:
American employers added 165,000 jobs in October, exceeding economists’ expectations after months of sluggish hiring, although economists warned that the rebound has yet to resolve broader weaknesses facing American workers.
The unemployment rate declined from 4.2% to 4.1%, while payroll growth exceeded economists’ expectations of approximately 59,000 jobs, according to figures released Friday by the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS). The improvement offered some relief following months of uncertainty about the labor market’s direction, but economists told the Daily Caller News Foundation that limited job opportunities, pressure on household finances and persistent inflation continue to weigh on Americans.
“October’s jobs report was more treat than trick, with hiring bouncing back after a ghoulish September,” Daniel Zhao, chief economist at Glassdoor, told the DCNF.
Private employers accounted for 159,000 of October’s new jobs, while government payrolls increased by 6,000. Professional and business services led private-sector gains, adding 70,000 positions, followed by health care with 42,000 and transportation and warehousing with 25,000. Manufacturing added 19,000 jobs, while construction shed approximately 3,000.
Within government, state payrolls increased by 8,000 jobs, driven by an increase of approximately 11,500 positions in state government education. Those gains were partially offset by the loss of approximately 2,600 jobs in other state government positions. Federal and local government employment each declined by approximately 1,000 positions, leaving overall government hiring relatively unchanged.
The report also revised hiring figures for August and September upward by a combined 84,000 jobs. August’s gain increased from 133,000 to 186,000, while September’s previously reported increase of 29,000 rose to 60,000. The revisions brought average monthly job growth over the past three months to approximately 137,000, the strongest pace since May.
Despite the improvement, Zhao cautioned that workers seeking employment continue to confront a difficult market, particularly those entering the workforce.
“Employers are still cautious about adding headcount, and early-career workers are feeling that the most,” Zhao told the DCNF.
Glassdoor’s employee confidence data showed that only approximately 43% of entry-level workers held a positive outlook toward their employers in October, compared with roughly 61% of employees at the director level and above. Confidence among entry-level workers declined 3.8 percentage points from a year earlier, the steepest drop of any seniority group, according to Zhao.
“In a low-hire market, it’s tough for young grads to get onto that ladder in the first place,” Zhao said. “October’s stronger hiring is a welcome sign, but it’ll take a few more months of momentum before entry-level workers will meaningfully feel the door opening.”
The official employment figures also revealed persistent difficulties for Americans unable to find work. Approximately 2 million people remained unemployed for at least 27 weeks, while the number of Americans working part time for economic reasons increased by 339,000 to 4.8 million.
The labor force participation rate edged up to 61.9%, while the number of unemployed Americans remained near 7.1 million.
Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody’s Analytics, told the DCNF ahead of Friday’s report that the principal threat to the economy would be an acceleration in layoffs rather than weak hiring alone.
“For the job market and broader economy to significantly falter, there would need to be a meaningful pickup in layoffs,” Zandi said.
He also warned that declining inflation-adjusted wages and low household savings threatened consumer spending, particularly if financial markets weakened.
The latest figures showed average hourly earnings increased 0.4% in October and 3.1% over the preceding 12 months. However, annual consumer price inflation reached 3.7% in September, according to previously released federal figures, outpacing the annual increase in nominal hourly wages reported Friday.
Cristian de Ritis, deputy chief economist at Moody’s Analytics, told the DCNF ahead of Friday’s report that the economy’s apparent resilience conceals growing financial divisions between wealthy and lower-income households.
“Spending can hold up as long as layoffs stay low and incomes keep growing,” de Ritis said. “But a labor market defined by both low hiring and low layoffs is increasingly fragile.”
Higher-income households account for nearly 60% of total consumer spending, according to Moody’s Analytics estimates cited by de Ritis. Their financial strength has helped sustain economic activity despite mounting pressure on less affluent Americans.
“Lower-income borrowers and those with weaker credit profiles are already showing strain on credit cards, auto loans, and student loans,” de Ritis said.
De Ritis warned that a deterioration in employment could broaden those financial difficulties, particularly among households with limited savings and little home equity.
“Consumers are not in crisis, but their buffer is wearing thin,” he said.
The October employment gains followed a period in which businesses largely retained existing employees while remaining hesitant to expand their workforces. September’s job openings report showed approximately 7.52 million vacancies nationwide, although a substantial share of the monthly increase came from state and local government employers rather than private businesses.
Zhao said October’s employment figures suggest the labor market remains resilient, but emphasized that a single strong report cannot establish a sustained recovery.
“We’ve seen strong months followed by disappointing ones this year, so the real test is whether employers can string a few of these months together,” Zhao told the DCNF.

sources.news_title: The U.S. Economy Added 165,000 Jobs in October, Beating Forecasts. Here's What That Could Mean for Interest Rates.
sources.text:
The U.S. economy added a seasonally adjusted 165,000 jobs in October, according to recently published data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS). That's well above the 59,000 economists had been expecting.
The unemployment rate fell slightly to 4.1%. Meanwhile, average hourly earnings increased 0.4% for the month and are up 3.1% year over year.
Strong monthly job gains were made in professional and business services (70,000); healthcare and social assistance (55,000); and transportation (24,800). Jobs were lost in leisure and hospitality (13,000), wholesale trade (9,100), and construction (3,000).
BLS also revised job gains from the prior two months meaningfully higher. The economy actually added 60,000 jobs in September, 31,000 higher than first reported. In August, gains actually totaled 186,000, 53,000 higher than first reported.
Here's what all of this means for interest rates.
Image source: Getty Images.
Strength in the economy
There's been lots of concern that high prices, stemming from the Iran war, may be pressuring the consumer, which makes up over two-thirds of U.S. gross domestic product. But the October jobs report shows the opposite.
"You have to look pretty hard to find something to dislike in there," Allianz Trade North America's Senior Economist Dan North said, according to CNBC. "It's a really, really good report, and all around I think you'd say it's stronger than expected and the best one in a while, and it kind of fits with what I call the stable but perhaps unexciting labor market."
US Nonfarm Payrolls MoM data by YCharts
In particular, the large gains in professional and business services generally reflect underlying economic strength, as many are high-paying jobs.
In prior reports, gains had largely come from healthcare and social assistance, which can grow at any point in the economic cycle.
Jobs reports can affect how the Federal Reserve sets interest rates because when people have jobs, they often have money to spend, and consumer spending accounts for the majority of U.S. GDP.
In recent years, there has been a bad-news-is-good-news mentality, in which investors have perceived strong jobs reports as negative because they are likely to lead to higher or persistently elevated inflation, forcing the Federal Reserve to hike interest rates, which can negatively impact stocks.
How does this impact the trajectory of the Fed?
To assess the probability of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) hiking rates, we can look at CME Group's FedWatch tool, which looks at 30-day futures to assign probabilities of what the FOMC will do at its upcoming meetings.
On Nov. 5, there was a nearly 67% chance the FOMC would hike rates at its final meeting of the year. Following the jobs report on Nov. 6, that number had jumped to over 78%.
So, the jobs report clearly made investors more worried about persistent inflation and led them to believe the Fed will act at its final meeting of the year. Looking ahead, investors now expect two more rate hikes between now and the end of 2027. Keep in mind these probabilities change frequently.
Truthfully, I wouldn't read too much into this report. Job reports and revisions have changed so frequently this year that it’s difficult to believe the data from one report alone.
Inflation data and the December jobs report between now and the FOMC’s December meeting could be completely different, changing the narrative. So, while the October report does support a Fed hike in December, a lot will likely happen between now and then.

Today: Accelerating growth of nonfarm payrolls & hourly earnings, historically low unemployment rate, very high prime-age labor force participation rate.

sources.text:
President Donald Trump just received another major piece of economic news, and this one blew straight past the experts.
America added 165,000 jobs in October while the unemployment rate fell to 4.1%, according to the latest employment report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Economists had expected roughly 65,000 new jobs, meaning the actual result beat the consensus forecast by about 100,000.
The details were even stronger than the headline number. Professional and business services added 70,000 jobs, manufacturing gained 19,000, and private-sector payrolls increased by 159,000.
Workers also saw their paychecks move in the right direction. Average hourly earnings rose 0.4% in October and were 4.0% higher than a year earlier.
The labor force expanded by 421,000 people while the number of unemployed Americans declined. That combination matters because it means the lower unemployment rate did not come from a mass exodus of workers.
The government also revised August and September upward by a combined 84,000 jobs. August was raised by 53,000 and September by 31,000, adding more evidence that the labor market entered the fall with greater momentum than first reported.
The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics released the October Employment Situation report.
— BLS-Labor Statistics (@BLS_gov) November 6, 2026
That is an emphatic answer to the people who spent months insisting the Trump economy was headed over a cliff.
They predicted tariffs would destroy American employment. They predicted the administration’s energy and deregulation policies would fail.
They predicted businesses would freeze hiring.
Instead, employers added more than twice the number of jobs economists expected, wages continued climbing, and unemployment moved lower.
The manufacturing gain is especially notable. For decades, Washington accepted the idea that America should ship factories abroad and then lecture displaced workers about a supposedly inevitable global economy.
Trump rejected that surrender. His agenda has focused on domestic production, fairer trade, lower energy costs, and making the United States a place where companies build things again.
One report does not settle every economic question, and Americans still feel the damage caused by years of inflation. Housing, groceries, insurance, and other essentials remain too expensive for millions of families.
But that is precisely why real wage growth and a healthy labor market matter. Families need more opportunity and bigger paychecks, not another Washington program that promises relief while quietly driving prices higher.
The October numbers also expose how quickly the media narrative can become detached from reality. Bad forecasts receive days of dramatic coverage, while strong results are often buried beneath caveats designed to make good news sound suspicious.
Americans can read the numbers for themselves: 165,000 jobs, 4.1% unemployment, rising wages, stronger prior months, and solid private-sector hiring.
The October jobs report surpassed expectations as unemployment declined.
— FOX Business (@FoxBusiness) November 6, 2026
The political class will argue over who deserves credit, but the direction is clear. Employers are hiring, more Americans are entering the workforce, and workers are earning more.
That does not mean the job is finished. It means the policies Washington was told could never work are producing results that the so-called experts failed to see coming.
For President Trump, this is more than a favorable headline. It is evidence that putting American workers, manufacturing, and economic independence first can deliver measurable gains.
And for the pundits who predicted disaster, October’s report is one more reminder: the American economy does not take its orders from the permanent bureaucracy.

US continues to generate jobs, yet inflation is eroding the spending power of millions of Americans
WASHINGTON (AP) — U.S. employers created a surprising 165,000 new jobs last month, and the unemployment rate dipped to 4.1%.
Hiring was far stronger than the 65,000 new jobs that economists had expected.
The jobs report comes three days after voters delivered a stunning defeat to President Donald Trump and his Republican Party in midterm elections. Frustrated with the state of the economy — and especially the high cost of living – Americans handed full control of Congress to the Democrats.
But the latest jobs report looked solid. Labor Department revisions added a combined 84,000 new jobs to the August and September totals.
The unemployment rate fell even though 421,000 people entered the labor force.
Average hourly wages rose 0.4% in October from September, the biggest month-over-month gain since January.
"This was a blowout jobs report,'' said Angelo Kourkafas, senior global strategist at Edward Jones. "Payroll growth exceeded expectations, revisions were positive, the unemployment rate fell, participation improved, and wage growth strengthened.''
Trending News
The strong job gains will likely make Federal Reserve policymakers more confident in the health of the labor market, giving them leeway to focus on persistently high inflation and raise their benchmark interest rate at their next meeting in December.
The central bank typically seeks to bring down inflation by lifting its key interest rate to cool borrowing and spending. The Fed raised the rate in September but left it alone at its meeting last month. Wall Street investors now see the chance of a December rate hike at 77%, up about 10 percentage points from Thursday, according to CME's FedWatch.
"For sure, we're looking at another rate increase in December and possibly another one in early 2027,'' said Boston College economist Brian Bethune.
Solid hiring also underscores a concern among many Fed officials that their key rate isn't high enough to slow inflation.
Hourly wages were up a meager 3.1% from October 2025. That means many workers have seen their purchasing power decline over the past year, despite continued hiring.
Professional and business services – a broad category of administrative and managerial workers – added 70,000 jobs. Healthcare companies hired nearly 42,000. Factories added 19,000 jobs. But hotels, restaurants and bars cut 10,600.
The job market has been solid but unspectacular.
So far this year, employers — companies, government agencies and nonprofits — have added an average of 86,000 jobs a month. That is modest by historic standards but an improvement over 2025, when monthly job creation averaged 9,700. That was the weakest performance outside of a recession since 2002. Last year, high interest rates and President Donald Trump's unpredictable trade policies discouraged hiring.
Despite recovering this year, hiring remains well below the average of 166,000 jobs created monthly in 2023 and 2024, let alone the 491,000 a month recorded during the 2021-2022 hiring boom that followed COVID-19 lockdowns.
Economists see a "low-hire, low-fire'' environment in which employers are reluctant to let go of existing workers but aren't in any hurry to hire new ones. Young people entering the workforce, or those who've lost their jobs, can struggle to find work.
The United States doesn't need as many new jobs as it once did to keep the unemployment rate from rising. That's because baby boomer retirements and Trump's immigration crackdown mean fewer people are competing for work.
In late 2023, the so-called break-even point was around 166,000 new jobs a month. It's now just over 5,000, according to an estimate by Yale University's Budget Lab, which drew on an earlier Federal Reserve report.
The American economy and job market have proven resilient in the face of a series of shocks — Trump's double-digit tariffs on imports and the war with Iran, which has driven U.S. gasoline prices above $4 a gallon and pinched family budgets.
Gross domestic product — the nation's output of goods and services — advanced at a sprightly 3.4% annual pace from July through September, lifted by strong consumer spending and booming investment in artificial intelligence.
But AI can also mean that businesses need fewer workers.
At SharkNinja in Needham, Massachusetts, sales jumped 21% in the latest quarter as budget-minded shoppers brought the company's appliances – such as coffee- and smoothie-makers-- to save money on dining out.
But CEO Mark Barrocas says he's slowed hiring – to 5% next year from 8% to 10% the previous two years. The reason: AI. SharkNinja, which has a total global workforce of 4,200, has implemented AI tools in such areas as product innovation, media planning and finance.
"It's allowing people to work on much higher-impact initiatives as opposed to more tedious tasks," he said. But AI has also created new jobs for people with expertise in using AI to increase efficiency.

The Jobs Report Just Changed the Math for Retirees. Here’s What a Rate Hike Means for a 67-Year-Old With $400,000 and Social Security.
A blowout jobs report is good news for the economy, but the same quarter point that pads a saver's interest can quietly drain a bond fund. Which side of the rate move you stand on decides whether Friday helped or…
The economy added 165,000 jobs in October, the Labor Department said Friday morning, more than double the roughly 65,000 that economists expected. The unemployment rate fell to 4.1%. The two prior months were revised up by a combined 84,000 jobs.
For anyone living on interest, this is the best news of a bad week. A job market this firm removes the Federal Reserve’s main reason to hold back, and within minutes of the report traders raised their bets that the Fed will lift interest rates again in December, Reuters reported. Here is what the report said, and what another rate increase is worth in dollars to a retiree, a bond fund owner and a worker.
What the report said
Hiring was strong and broad. Professional and business services added 70,000 jobs, far above that sector’s average of 15,000 a month over the past year, and manufacturing added 19,000. Unemployment at 4.1% is down from 4.2% in September and from 4.5% last November.
Pay was the weak spot. Average hourly earnings rose 3.1% from a year earlier, to $38.00. Consumer prices rose 3.7% over the 12 months through September, according to the government’s price index. That likely makes seven straight months in which wages trailed inflation, The Wall Street Journal noted.
Why this points to a December rate increase
The Fed raised rates in September for the first time since 2023, to a range of 3.75% to 4.00%, and held them there in October. Inflation is running almost two points above its 2% target. The usual argument for waiting is a weakening job market, and Friday’s report took that argument away. The Fed’s next decision comes in December.
What a rate increase is worth to a saver
Take a 67-year-old retiree with $400,000 in Treasury bills, CDs and a money market fund, on top of a Social Security check. The three-month Treasury bill yields 4.21%, according to Treasury data. At that rate her savings earn $16,840 a year, or about $1,400 a month.
For most of this year that income has barely kept up. Inflation at 3.7% takes about $14,950 of buying power out of $400,000 in a year, so after inflation she came out ahead by roughly $1,900. One more quarter-point increase adds $1,000 a year to her interest, about $83 a month, and lifts that margin to nearly $2,900. Social Security is adjusted for inflation once a year. Her savings only get a raise when the Fed gives one, and Friday made that more likely.
The catch is at the bank. A savings account paying 0.5% earns $2,000 a year on the same $400,000. The $14,840 gap between that and a Treasury bill is larger than anything the Fed will do in December. Where the money sits matters more than the next rate move.
What it costs a bond fund owner
The same news cuts the other way for bonds she already owns. When rates rise, existing bonds fall in price, and the rule of thumb is simple: a fund’s price drops by about its duration, in years, times the rise in rates. A typical intermediate-term bond fund has a duration near six years. A quarter-point increase in yields takes about 1.5% off its price, or $3,000 on a $200,000 holding.
She is not being paid much to take that risk. The 10-year Treasury yields 4.90% and the two-year 4.58%, against 4.21% for a three-month bill. Lending to the government for ten years instead of three months earns an extra 0.69 of a point, about $1,380 a year on $200,000, and one quarter-point move against her erases more than two years of that.
What it means if you are still working
The average wage of $38.00 an hour comes to $79,040 a year for full-time work. A 3.1% raise on that is $2,450. Keeping up with 3.7% inflation would have taken $2,954. The average worker got a raise and still lost about $500 of buying power, which is why a report this strong will not feel like good news in most households.
What to watch before December
Three numbers come before the Fed meets: October’s inflation report, one more jobs report, and what Fed officials say in between. If inflation stays near 3.7% and hiring holds, a December increase is the base case. For a saver, that argues for keeping maturities short for now, so the money can be reinvested at the higher rate. For a bond fund owner, it argues for knowing your fund’s duration before the meeting, not after.
The bottom line
A report showing 165,000 new jobs and 4.1% unemployment makes a December rate increase more likely. For a retiree with $400,000 in short-term savings, each quarter point is worth $1,000 a year, on top of the $16,840 she earns now. For a $200,000 intermediate bond fund, the same quarter point costs about $3,000 in price. And for the average worker, a 3.1% raise against 3.7% inflation still left a $500 hole. Good news for the economy lands differently depending on which side of the interest rate you are on.

By PAUL WISEMAN. AP Economics Writer
WASHINGTON (AP) — U.S. employers created a surprising 165,000 new jobs last month, and the unemployment rate dipped to 4.1%.
Hiring was far stronger than the 65,000 new jobs that economists had expected.
The jobs report comes three days after voters delivered a stunning defeat to President Donald Trump and his Republican Party in midterm elections. Frustrated with the state of the economy — and especially the high cost of living – Americans handed full control of Congress to the Democrats.
But the latest jobs report looked solid. Labor Department revisions added a combined 84,000 new jobs to the August and September totals.
The unemployment rate fell even though 421,000 people entered the labor force.
Average hourly wages rose 0.4% in October from September, the biggest month-over-month gain since January.
“This was a blowout jobs report,” said Angelo Kourkafas, senior global strategist at Edward Jones. “Payroll growth exceeded expectations, revisions were positive, the unemployment rate fell, participation improved, and wage growth strengthened.”
The strong job gains will likely make Federal Reserve policymakers more confident in the health of the labor market, giving them leeway to focus on persistently high inflation and raise their benchmark interest rate at their next meeting in December.
The central bank typically seeks to bring down inflation by lifting its key interest rate to cool borrowing and spending. The Fed raised the rate in September but left it alone at its meeting last month. Wall Street investors now see the chance of a December rate hike at 77%, up about 10 percentage points from Thursday, according to CME’s FedWatch.
“For sure, we’re looking at another rate increase in December and possibly another one in early 2027,’’ said Boston College economist Brian Bethune.
Solid hiring also underscores a concern among many Fed officials that their key rate isn’t high enough to slow inflation.
Hourly wages were up a meager 3.1% from October 2025. That means many workers have seen their purchasing power decline over the past year, despite continued hiring.
Professional and business services – a broad category of administrative and managerial workers – added 70,000 jobs. Healthcare companies hired nearly 42,000. Factories added 19,000 jobs. But hotels, restaurants and bars cut 10,600.
The job market has been solid but unspectacular.
So far this year, employers — companies, government agencies and nonprofits — have added an average of 86,000 jobs a month. That is modest by historic standards but an improvement over 2025, when monthly job creation averaged 9,700. That was the weakest performance outside of a recession since 2002. Last year, high interest rates and President Donald Trump’s unpredictable trade policies discouraged hiring.
Despite recovering this year, hiring remains well below the average of 166,000 jobs created monthly in 2023 and 2024, let alone the 491,000 a month recorded during the 2021-2022 hiring boom that followed COVID-19 lockdowns.
Economists see a “low-hire, low-fire’’ environment in which employers are reluctant to let go of existing workers but aren’t in any hurry to hire new ones. Young people entering the workforce, or those who’ve lost their jobs, can struggle to find work.
The United States doesn’t need as many new jobs as it once did to keep the unemployment rate from rising. That’s because baby boomer retirements and Trump’s immigration crackdown mean fewer people are competing for work.

Employment conditions strengthened in October as job growth blew past economists’ forecasts and the unemployment rate unexpectedly fell.
The economy added 165,000 new jobs last month, from an upwardly revised 60,000 in September, according to data released by the Bureau of Labor Statistics on Nov. 6.
The consensus forecast suggested a gain of 65,000.
October’s unemployment rate dipped to 4.1 percent—below the market estimate—from 4.2 percent the previous month.
New payroll data reaffirm the U.S. labor market’s resilience amid several headwinds, from elevated inflation to ongoing tariffs.
In addition to last month’s solid reading, the bureau revised previous months higher. September’s gain was revised up by 31,000, from 29,000 to 60,000. August’s count was also adjusted by 53,000, from 133,000 to 186,000.
Year-to-date, the economy has created 861,000 jobs, far higher than the 116,000 added in all of 2025.
“The economy is doing well,” Chris Zaccarelli, chief investment officer at Northlight Asset Management, told The Epoch Times in an emailed note.
Last month’s job growth, meanwhile, came almost entirely from the private sector, as government payrolls rose by just 6,000.
Employment gains were also broad-based, led by professional and business services (70,000), healthcare (42,000), transportation and warehousing (25,000), and manufacturing (19,000). Over the last couple of years, healthcare has been a key driver of job growth in the United States.
Nominal wages came in above expectations, with average hourly earnings rising 0.4 percent last month. On a 12-month basis, average hourly earnings eased to a higher-than-expected 3.1 percent.
Employed full-time workers surged by 714,000, while part-time employment slipped by 242,000. Self-employed workers declined by more than 100,000.
For the third straight month, the workforce participation rate edged up to 61.9 percent, the highest since March. More than 400,000 people entered the labor force.
This week’s tranche of employment highlighted persistently low layoffs. Unemployment claims were at a 57-year low, and planned job cuts in October fell 71 percent from a year ago. But the latest nonfarm payrolls report suggests hiring momentum could be picking up heading into the busy holiday season.
“Today’s jobs report, which blew past expectations and added 165,000 jobs, is proof that President Trump’s pro-growth economic agenda is working,” White House spokesman Matthew Middleton said in a statement.
“From almost 20 fair trade deals to trillions in manufacturing investments, this administration is putting America back on a path to prosperity. President Trump’s mission remains unchanged: lowering costs, creating jobs, boosting our economy, and putting American workers first.”
One Less Worry for the Fed
With the Federal Reserve focused primarily on the price stability side of its dual mandate, a strong October jobs report provides the Federal Reserve with one less worry when crafting monetary policy.
But this also means higher interest rates, says Larry Holzenthaler, senior portfolio manager at Catalyst Funds.
“This clearly sets the Fed up very well to continue to bring their target rate higher to address inflation. Our view remains that the Fed needs to continue to bring rates higher,” Holzenthaler said in an emailed note to The Epoch Times.
The Fed left interest rates unchanged last month following its first rate hike in more than three years in September. Futures markets overwhelmingly expect the central bank to raise rates by a quarter point at the Dec. 8–9 meeting.
U.S. Treasury bond yields were mostly up, with the benchmark 10-year inching closer to 4.9 percent.
Following its worst day in 19 months, U.S. stocks were mixed after the October payroll data.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index rose about 400 points, or 1.5 percent. Conversely, the blue-chip Dow Jones Industrial Average erased around 500 points, or nearly 1 percent. The broad-market S&P 500 was little changed.
Holiday Hiring
Hiring could kick into high gear with the economy entering the busy holiday season.
Seasonal hiring got off to a hot start when Amazon said it would hire 300,000 U.S. workers, up by 50,000 from each of the last three years. UPS also announced 100,000 seasonal hires.
In October, seasonal hiring plans surged 26 percent from a year ago, topping about 470,000, according to global outplacement firm Challenger, Gray and Christmas.
“Employers are holding on to the workers they have heading into the holidays, and the hiring they are announcing is largely short-term, seasonal work. Companies want the flexibility to meet holiday demand without adding permanent headcount,” Andy Challenger, chief revenue officer for Challenger, Gray and Christmas, said in a statement.
Despite demand for labor remaining elevated—holiday-related or not—the percentage of people unemployed for an extended period remains high.
The long-term unemployment rate—individuals out of work for 27 weeks or more as a share of total unemployed—was 27.6 percent, from 27.1 percent in September.

sources.news_title: The US economy added 165,000 jobs in October and the unemployment rate fell
sources.text:
Job growth surpassed expectations in October, new data showed Friday, with the US economy adding 165,000 jobs.
The unemployment rate fell to 4.1% from 4.2%, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data.
Job growth in the previous two months was stronger than initially reported, with a total of 84,000 jobs added: August was revised upwards by 53,000 to 186,000; and September gains totaled 60,000, up from 29,000.
The consensus forecast for October called for monthly gains of 65,000 jobs and a 4.2% unemployment rate, FactSet estimates show.
Friday’s report well exceeded those expectations and painted a picture of a labor market that’s not just resilient and stable – but one that’s robust.
“Today’s jobs report is a strong rebuttal to fears that the economy is heading into a meaningful slowdown,” Seema Shah, chief global strategist at Principal Asset Management, wrote Friday.
Through October, job growth is averaging 86,100 per month. That’s a breath of fresh air from the sub-10,000 jobs per month added last year; still, the gains this year are still running below 2024 and pre-pandemic levels, when monthly job gains averaged roughly 120,000.
However, when looking at recent months, the pace of job growth is looking much more formidable: Barring future revisions, the three-month average for US employment gains is 137,000 jobs, BLS data shows. The unemployment rate has been at or under 4.5% for a record 60* months in a row (*the BLS did not report an unemployment rate for October 2025 due to the government shutdown).
Beyond the stronger-than-expected headline numbers, Friday’s report also showed that job growth occurred across a broader suite of industries.
The bulk of October’s gains occurred in the professional and business services sector, which added 70,000 jobs. The healthcare and social assistance industry, which has kept the labor market afloat in recent years, added 55,100 jobs last month.
Other solid gains were reported in durable goods manufacturing (+25,000), a sector that’s been boosted in part by AI-related investment; transportation and warehousing (+24,500), a sector that’s gearing up for the holiday shopping season; and temporary help services (+18,600), a “canary in the coalmine” sector that shows employers might be testing the waters before making a permanent hire.
Tyler Schipper, associate professor of economics at St. Thomas University in Saint Paul, Minnesota, cautioned that some of those categories have been “noisy” in recent months.
Still a low-churn environment
The burst of optimism, however, comes with some caveats.
“Part of my hesitance comes from, if we look at the three-month average of job growth right now, it’s pretty similar to where it was earlier in the year,” he said. “And then it dropped back down pretty dramatically over the summer and the early fall.”
“So, is this the beginning of a trend, or are we going to see what we saw earlier this year, where things pick up and then they drop off a little bit,” he added.
The recent months’ job gains as well as Indeed’s job postings in September, which notched the first year-over-year gain in four years, are certainly encouraging data points, he said; however, those don’t decisively change the trajectory of a slow-churn labor market that’s been firmly entrenched in a “low-hire, low-fire” state for years.
It’s been a labor market that’s worked for some but not all, especially younger workers and unemployed Americans looking to reenter the labor market. In October, unemployment duration rose to its highest level since December 2021, he said.
“But even workers who have jobs, they’re maybe not losing those jobs, but they’re also potentially having a hard time right now, because wage growth has been pretty mild, especially relative to inflation,” he said.
In October, wage growth slowed on an annual basis to 3.1% from an upwardly revised 3.2%. Americans’ pay gains are hovering around pre-pandemic levels; however, inflation is not: Prices have been rising faster in recent months, driven higher by a war-driven energy shock.
The cost of living remains a major concern for households, while employers are navigating demographic shifts, the rapid adoption of AI, persistently elevated inflation and the war with Iran. And a job market that appears healthy does not necessarily feel that way to workers.
The better-than-expected hiring offers some reassurance for an economy entering a new political chapter after the Democrats’ sweep in the midterm elections.

sources.news_title: U.S. economy added 165,000 jobs in October, way more than expected; unemployment rate slips to 4.1%
sources.text:
The U.S. economy added jobs at a much stronger-than-expected pace in October, while the unemployment rate moved lower as the labor market showed surprising strength.
Nonfarm payrolls increased by a seasonally adjusted 165,000 for the month, compared with the Dow Jones estimate for 59,000, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Friday.
The unemployment rate nudged down to 4.1%, compared with the forecast for 4.2%. A more encompassing measure that includes discouraged workers and those holding part-time jobs for economic reasons rose to 7.9%, up 0.3 percentage point, amid an increase of 421,000 in the civilian labor force.
In addition to the strong payroll gains for October, prior months were revised up substantially: The August figure moved to 186,000, an upward revision of 53,000, while the September count shifted to 60,000 following an upward revision of 31,000.
"You have to look pretty hard to find something to dislike in there," Dan North, senior economist at Allianz Trade North America. "It's a really, really good report, and all around I think you'd say it's stronger than expected and the best one in a while, and it kind of fits with what I call the stable but perhaps unexciting labor market."
Payroll gains also came in better than forecast. Average hourly earnings increased 0.4% on the month and 3.1% annually, compared with respective estimates for 0.3% and 2.9%. The average workweek was unchanged at 34.4 hours.
"Today's jobs report is a strong rebuttal to fears that the economy is heading into a meaningful slowdown," said Seema Shah, chief global strategist at Principal Asset Management. "Payrolls growth surprised firmly to the upside, unemployment fell back to 4.1%, and job creation remains broad-based, pointing to an economy that is still absorbing labor comfortably rather than one beginning to buckle under tighter financial conditions."
The breadth of job growth also was strong, contrary to a trend in which healthcare had accounted for the bulk of gains.
Professional and business services saw an increase of 70,000 to lead all sectors, while healthcare was next at 42,000. Other areas seeing notable growth included transportation and warehousing (25,000) and manufacturing (19,000).
"The overall picture is a labor market that is on much better footing than a year ago," said Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union. "In 2025, the economy added barely 10,000 jobs a month and basically all were in healthcare. ... There's a much more broad based range of opportunities."
The report comes the same week as an election in which the economy and in particular inflation were the center of attention. Democrats staged a nationwide rout that will give the party control of both chambers of Congress after campaigning heavily on addressing affordability issues.
For the Federal Reserve, the report also comes at a pivotal time. Central bankers are weighing whether to resume raising interest rates in December as inflation remains stubbornly above the central bank's 2% target.
Traders increased the probability of another quarter percentage point hike when the Federal Open Market Committee meets Dec. 8-9. Odds rose to 76.8%, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool, though the indicator pointed to only one more increase after. The odds of further hikes in 2027 have fallen somewhat in recent days, after the midterm election rout and Thursday's sell-off in tech stocks.
Market reaction otherwise was muted, with a mixed picture on stock market futures heading into the open. Treasury yields were higher across the board.
The share of workers either looking for a job or already working as a share of the workforce, known as the labor force participation rate, edged higher to 61.9%. The labor force had been shrinking, the result of demographic changes and immigration reductions, but expanded by 421,000 in October.
At the same time, the household report, which is used to calculate the unemployment rate, showed 463,000 more people at work.
Long-term unemployment, though, rose sharply.
The average duration of unemployment jumped to 27.1 weeks, up 2.3 weeks from the prior month to the highest since September 2021. Those unemployed for more than 27 weeks increased to 1.96 million, the most since December 2021.

U.S. adds 156,000 jobs in October, unemployment steady at 4.1% - The Daily Bo Snerdley
sources.text:
(The Center Square) – The U.S. economy added 156,000 jobs in October and unemployment remained steady at 4.1%, according to a new report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics released Friday.
The unemployment rate has remained in a narrow range between 4.1% and 4.3% since March. Employment in professional and business services shot up by 70,000 in the month of October, well above the 15,000 job monthly average over the last year.
Orphe Divounguy, The Center Square’s chief economist, expected lower growth in October. He estimated an additional 86,000 jobs, well below what the bureau reported.
Healthcare, a reliable hiring industry, exceeded expectations with an additional 42,000 jobs in October. On average, the industry recruited 31,000 jobs per month over the last year.
The transportation and warehousing industry added 25,000 jobs in October, driven by couriers and messengers. Divounguy said the industry is an important one to keep an eye on as hiring increases ahead of the holiday season.
“The important comparison is whether they hire more or fewer workers than usual for this season.,” Divounguy told The Center Square. “Because the headline figures adjust for normal seasonal patterns, employers can add holiday workers while recording a seasonally adjusted decline if hiring falls short of the usual buildup.”
The transportation and warehousing industry added 104,000 jobs since a recent low in February, according to the report.
Average hourly earnings increased by 14 cents or 0.4% in October, allowing wage growth to tick up slightly to 3.1%. Divounguy said inflation remains a core issue for meaningful wage growth.
“For households, the problem is that inflation has outpaced those gains: inflation-adjusted hourly earnings were down 0.7% from a year earlier in September,” Divounguy said.
Long-term unemployment accounted for 27.6% of all unemployed people. Roughly two million people have been jobless for 27 weeks or more, according to the report.
“Long-term unemployment concerns me most,” Divounguy said. “If you are out of a job, finding one has become difficult, and more people risk getting stuck in unemployment for longer.”
The labor force participation rate, at 61.9%, changed little from January. The participation rate of prime-age adults remained consistent over the last several months.
“Those figures support my view of a broadly stable labor market for workers in their prime working years,” Divounguy said. “Monthly household-survey figures can swing, so I’ll watch whether these gains hold over the next few reports rather than read too much into any one month.”

AI Spending and Hiring Are Driving the Economy As Jobs Growth for October Is 'Unexpectedly' High
sources.text:
The jobs report reflects a growing disconnect between the public's perception that AI will be bad for the economy and their personal job situation, and the reality that AI is driving a genuine economic boom.
The jobs picture brightened considerably in October.
"Employers added 165,000 jobs last month, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Friday, and the unemployment rate dropped to 4.1 percent," reports The New York Times. "Job gains for August and September were revised upward by a total of 84,000 positions. Average hourly earnings rose 3.1 percent compared with the same time last year."
Layoffs are at historically low levels. Employees have also been reluctant to leave their jobs. Does this mean that the doom and gloom predictions about AI were wrong?
Naysayers believe it's premature to say one way or another what AI's effect on jobs will eventually be. But we know that the AI buildout underway, where trillions of dollars are being spent by businesses, has initiated a genuine economic boom.
The latest report released by the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) showed real gross domestic product (GDP) increased at an annualized rate of 3.4% in the third quarter of 2026. The 3.4% growth rate beat consensus expectations (which hovered around 3.2%) and marked an acceleration from the 2.2% growth recorded in the second quarter.
"The Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey this week showed that the quits rate rose in September, a sign that workers may be feeling more confident in their ability to get new jobs, The Times reports. That may mean a boost in hiring is on the way.
Another positive indication that reflects AI's impact on the overall economy is the surge in data center construction that Democrats and some Republicans want to shut down. Fears of that possibility drove stocks into the ground with a massive sell-off on Wednesday.
But even Democrats won't kill the goose that lays the golden eggs.
Skanda Amarnath, executive director of Employ America, estimated that the spending categories most tied to the AI boom contributed to “well over 7.5% of GDP.” And it’s still growing at a rapid clip: AI-related capital expenditures drove 13% of the growth in total nonresidential business fixed investment from the second quarter to the third quarter, according to Abiel Reinhart, a senior economist at JPMorgan Chase.
Investors may settle down over the next few days, concluding that whatever restraints might be coming on AI, particularly at the state level, will merely result in a mild slowdown. But the jitters aren’t likely to go away.
“This is a moment for getting policy right,” said Adam Kovacevich, founder and CEO of the center-left industry coalition Chamber of Progress. Kovacevich noted that many Democrats don’t support a total shutdown of data center construction. “American AI companies are powering the stock market, people’s retirement accounts, their pensions. The data center buildout is putting a lot of Americans to work.”
So what impact has AI actually had in real time on the job market?
White-collar industries like accounting, legal services and finance mostly added jobs in October, but their growth has been decidedly weak over the past few years. The information sector — a broad category that includes much of tech but also media companies — has been cutting jobs steadily since late 2022. Microsoft last week announced that it was offering buyouts to tens of thousands of employees, making it the latest tech giant to cut jobs.
Economists are cautious about attributing that softness to A.I., however. Other forces, such as high interest rates and shifting demand patterns following the pandemic, could also be playing a role. And despite announcements like Microsoft’s, layoffs remain low, even in white-collar sectors.
There are some indications that AI is displacing entry-level workers. But that could be a reflection of massive increases in minimum wages at the state level and the fact that the low rate of turnover is keeping entry-level jobs from opening up.
"The impact of A.I. is showing up clearly in one place, however: blue-collar jobs," notes the Times. "The data center build-out is helping to prop up employment in the construction sector, even as high interest rates have led to a sharp pullback in home building."
In fact, the irony is that electing all these Democrats may lead to a slowdown in all aspects of the AI build-out that would bring economic growth to a screeching halt. And Trump knows exactly where the blame will lie.
Some economists and AI prognosticators still predict an AI bubble that will burst when sky-high profit expectations aren't met and investment in the AI buildout slows dramatically. That may not happen, as investors are becoming more realistic about the near-term prospects for AI-driven profits.
Businesses thrive on certainty. The current business climate is so uncertain that, as my grandfather used to say about arriving in the U.S. in the 1880s, "It's good to be shifty in a new country."
Those who recognize opportunity and adapt quickly will thrive.

sources.news_title: U.S. economy adds 165,000 jobs in October; jobless rate dips to 4.1%
sources.text:
U.S. employers created a surprising 165,000 new jobs last month and the unemployment rate dipped to 4.1 per cent.
The hiring was far stronger than the 65,000 new jobs that economists had expected.
Labor Department revisions added 84,000 new jobs in August and September.
The unemployment rate fell even though 421,000 people entered the labour force.
But hourly wages rose a meagre 3.1 per cent from October 2025, with many families struggling to keep up with inflation.
Professional and business services – a broad category of administrative and managerial workers – added 70,000. Healthcare companies hired nearly 42,000. Factories added 19,000 jobs. But hotels, restaurants and bars cut 10,600.
The jobs report arrives three days after voters handed a stunning defeat to President Donald Trump and his Republican Party in midterm elections. Frustrated with the state of the economy – and especially the high cost of living – Americans handed full control of the U.S. Congress to the Democrats.
Yet the American economy and job market have proven resilient in the face of a series of shocks – Trump’s double-digit taxes on imports and the war with Iran, which has driven U.S. gasoline prices above $4 a gallon and pinched family budgets.
Gross domestic product – the nation’s output of goods and services – advanced at a sprightly 3.4-per-cent annual pace from July through September, lifted by strong consumer spending and booming investment in artificial intelligence.
The job market has been solid but unspectacular.
So far this year, employers – companies, government agencies and nonprofits – have added an average of 68,000 jobs a month, including a disappointing 29,000 last month. That is modest by historic standards but an improvement over 2025 when monthly job creation averaged 9,700. That was the weakest performance outside of a recession since 2002. Last year, high interest rates and President Donald Trump’s unpredictable trade policies discouraged hiring.
Despite recovering this year, hiring remains well below the average of 166,000 monthly jobs created in 2023 and 2024, let alone the 491,000 a month recorded during the 2021-2022 hiring boom that followed COVID-19 lockdowns.
Economists see a “low-fire, low-hire’’ environment in which employers are reluctant to let go of existing workers but aren’t in any hurry to hire new ones. Young people entering the work force, or those who’ve lost their jobs, can struggle to find work.
The United States doesn’t need as many new jobs as it once did to keep the unemployment rate from rising. That is because baby boomer retirements and Trump’s immigration crackdown mean fewer people are competing for work.
In late 2023, the so-called break-even point was around 166,000 new jobs a month. It’s now just over 5,000, according to an estimate by Yale University’s Budget Lab, which drew on an earlier Federal Reserve report.
Meanwhile, rising prices have pinched pay for millions of Americans. After taking inflation into account, average hourly earnings fell 0.7 per cent in September – the sixth straight year-over-year drop and one explanation for voters’ fury at the polls Tuesday.

“The strains in this report stem from the key issue of the just-completed midterm elections,” Hamrick, founder of The Hamrick Brief personal finance website, said via email. “Average hourly earnings are up 3.1% over the past year, while inflation has been running well ahead of that figure. That affordability gap is putting distance between what Americans can afford and what they'd like to achieve with their personal finances.”
The latest consumer price index, a popular measure of inflation, showed prices increased at an annual rate of 3.7% in September. October’s CPI is scheduled to be released next week.
Hamrick said his site has a tool for people to see how their pay fares relative to prices.
Hamrick said Friday’s jobs report keeps an interest rate hike on the table next month for Federal Reserve officials.
The Fed has a dual mandate of price stability and maximum employment. That means keeping inflation in check and Americans working.

Hamrick said Fed officials will look at the new jobs report and “continue to believe that the employment side of their dual mandate is in sufficiently acceptable shape.”
Economists expected job growth of 59,000 in October. Instead, they got 165,000.

US adds 165,000 jobs, topping all forecasts in broad advance
U.S. job growth surged in October and the unemployment rate edged lower, signs of labor-market strength in an expanding economy.
Nonfarm payrolls increased 165,000 last month, topping all forecasts, after an upward revision to the prior two months, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data out Friday. The unemployment rate fell to 4.1%.
Employers across a broad range of sectors added jobs, including in professional and business services, healthcare and manufacturing. Overall private-sector payroll growth was the strongest since March.
Resilient consumer spending and strong business investment have supported demand and boosted corporate profits this year, encouraging companies to add more workers. Job growth has been uneven from month to month, but overall hiring has been strong enough to keep the unemployment rate at or below 4.5% for five years, the longest such stretch on record.
Federal Reserve officials will see one more jobs report and a full slate of inflation data before their next meeting in December. Investors expect them to raise interest rates at that gathering to counter inflation, following an increase in September and a subsequent decision to leave rates unchanged in October.
“The report was broadly strong,” said Oscar Munoz, head of U.S. economics at TD Securities. “This should allow the Fed to continue focusing on inflation and what’s happening in financial markets.”
If sustained, solid job growth “would bode well not only for the labor market, but also for consumption and for spending,” he added.
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh last week described employment conditions as “quite positive” and said the central bank was focused on prices. The yield on 2-year Treasury notes rose and the S&P 500 was higher following the release.
Healthcare and social assistance employers added about 55,000 workers to payrolls in October, the most in six months. That sector has been the biggest driver of job growth in recent years.
Spending on data centers and demand for AI-related infrastructure has supported construction and manufacturing employment this year. Friday’s report showed that nonresidential construction firms continued to add jobs, even as broader construction payrolls were weighed down by losses in residential building.
Factory headcount also saw solid gains, with computer and electronic product manufacturing firms adding the most jobs in four years.
“The economy has been growing above trend, and even as businesses place greater emphasis on productivity, technology and disciplined headcount management, they continue to hire where demand warrants it,” EY-Parthenon’s Gregory Daco and Lydia Boussour said in a note.
Employment in the information and financial activities sectors, which have seen some of the fastest rates of job loss and AI adoption this year, showed tentative signs of stabilization in October.
Goldman Sachs Group Inc. economists, in a note published this week, said “AI’s labor market impact has become increasingly visible in recent months,” with “higher adoption associated with weaker job growth and higher unemployment” across nonmanufacturing industries.
The report also suggested the labor market is generating little wage pressure. Average hourly earnings advanced 3.1% from a year earlier, matching the slowest pace since 2021. On a monthly basis, however, they rose 0.4%, topping forecasts.
The wage figures highlight a key source of voter frustration in this week’s midterm elections. While the unemployment rate has been low, pay hasn’t kept up with inflation throughout most of 2026.
The participation rate – the share of the population that is working or actively looking for work – edged up to 61.9% in October, the highest since March. A broad measure of unemployment also rose as the ranks of those working part-time for economic reasons jumped to a six-month high.
Measures of long-term unemployment worsened, with the median duration of a jobless spell reaching 11.9 weeks, the longest since 2021. Labor-market turnover has been historically low for much of the last few years, which has made it difficult to find new jobs and led many to feel either locked out or stuck in place.
The payroll numbers have seen wild swings this year from month to month, with sometimes large deviations from economists’ estimates. The median forecast in Bloomberg’s survey for the October report was off by 95,000, and four other reports this year have seen misses at least as large.
Separate data out Friday showed U.S. consumer sentiment rose in early November to a three-month high.

US Jobs Soar By 165K Blowing Away Estimates; Unemployment Rate Drops Putting Dec Rate Hike Back In Play
In our preview of the October jobs report, we said that the labor data has rarely looked this solid going into a monthly payrolls report: claims near 57-year lows, the lowest October layoffs since 2023, JOLTS openings up 333K and ADP above expectations. If anything, the risk is to the upside of the 63K consensus, and the unemployment rate could well tick down.
Which, as we noted, was the problem as "a strong print gives Warsh, Hammack and Barkin all the cover they need to hike in December, right as the Nasdaq is coming off its worst day since March 2020. Goldman's rates desk thinks a single print can't take the hikes out." We said that we agree with this take, and added that the more likely outcome is a decent number that puts December back in play and adds a rates problem to what has so far been an AI problem. Given where positioning is, CTAs already selling and long-only "frozen (again)," that's not a recipe for a relief rally.
Well, moments ago, the BLS reported the October jobs and it came extremely red hot, enough to indeed put a December rate hike back on the docket, AI collapse notwithstanding. Here are the numbers:
October monthly payrolls rose by 165K, up more than double the 70K expected bounce, and the third highest print of 2026 (this was once again driven by private jobs, which surged by 159K, smashing expectations of 65K; government only accounted for 6K jobs in October).
The number was so hot it not only printed above the highest Wall Street estimate...
... it was a 5-sigma beat to the median consensus number.
Not only was October red hot, prior month revision were all higher: the August was revised up by 53,000, from +133,000  to +186,000, and September was revised up by 31,000, from +29,000 to +60,000. With these revisions, employment in August and September combined is 84,000 higher than previously 
reported. 
While the payrolls number was red hot, the monthly worker change blew it away, as 463K workers were added according to the Household survey, the third consecutive month of 400K+ workers added...
... which in turn helped the persistently lagging total worker series catch up every closer to the much stronger, in recent years, payrolls series.
Just as remarkable is that after years of chronic underperformance by full-time jobs, in October the number of full-time jobs soared by 714K, the second highest monthly increase in 2026, while par-time jobs plunged by 242K.
The one blemish in the report was that after a year of declining foreign-born workers, in October we saw 809K foreign-born workers added, the biggest increase since Jan 2025, while native-born workers dropped by 64K.
It wasn't just the job numbers that came in red hot: the unemployment rate unexpectedly dipped back to 4.1% from 4.2%, and against expectations of an unchanged print.
Among the major worker groups, the unemployment rates showed little or no change in October for adult men (3.9%), adult women (3.6%), teenagers (13.9%), and people who are White (3.7%), Black (6.6%), Asian (2.8 percent), or Hispanic (4.7 percent).
Both the labor force participation rate, at 61.9%, and the employment-population ratio, at 59.3%, changed little in October. These measures have shown little net change since January.
And completing the trifecta of hot data was the average hourly earnings which beat expectations both MoM and YoY, with the former printing 0.4%, above the 0.3% expected, and the highest since Nov 2025, while the annual change in earnings disappointed expectations of the first sub-3% print since covid, and instead rose from the pre-revision 3.0% to 3.1% (then again Sept was revised higher to 3.2%).
The average workweek for all employees on private nonfarm payrolls remained at 34.4 hours in October. In manufacturing, the average workweek was unchanged at 40.5 hours, and overtime edged up by 0.1 hour to 3.1 hours. The average workweek for production and nonsupervisory employees on private nonfarm payrolls declined by 0.1 hour to 33.8 hours.
Some more details from the report:
- The number of long-term unemployed (those jobless for 27 weeks or more), at 2.0 million, changed little over the month. The long-term unemployed accounted for 27.6 percent of all unemployed people.
- The number of people employed part time for economic reasons increased by 339,000 to 4.8 million in October. These individuals would have preferred full-time employment but were working part time because their hours had been reduced or they were unable to find full-time jobs.
- In October, the number of people not in the labor force who currently want a job changed little at 6.0 million. These individuals were not counted as unemployed because they were not actively looking for work during the 4 weeks preceding the survey or were unavailable to take a job.
- Among those not in the labor force who wanted a job, the number of people marginally attached to the labor force changed little at 1.6 million in October. These individuals wanted and were available for work and had looked for a job sometime in the prior 12 months but had not looked for work in the 4 weeks preceding the survey. The number of discouraged workers, a subset of the marginally attached who believed that no jobs were available for them, also changed little over the month at 448,000.
Looking at the composition of the October jobs print, we find the following:
- Employment in professional and business services increased by 70,000 in October, well above the average monthly gain of 15,000 over the prior 12 months. In October, employment continued to trend up in professional, scientific, and technical services (+33,000), in administrative and support and waste management and remediation services (+28,000), and in management of companies and enterprises (+9,000). Professional and business services has added 269,000 jobs since a recent low in October 2025.
- Health care added 42,000 jobs in October, higher than the average monthly gain of 31,000 over the prior 12 months. In October, employment gains occurred in hospitals (+16,000), home health care services (+11,000), and outpatient care centers (+5,000).
- In October, transportation and warehousing added 25,000 jobs, reflecting growth in couriers and messengers (+17,000) and air transportation (+4,000). Transportation and warehousing has added 104,000 jobs since a recent employment low in February, with couriers and messengers (+71,000) contributing most of the gain.
- Manufacturing employment continued to trend up in October (+19,000) and has increased by 101,000 since a recent low in December 2025. In October, job gains occurred in computer and electronic product manufacturing (+7,000), machinery manufacturing (+4,000), and primary metal manufacturing (+4,000).
Employment showed little change over the month in other major industries, including mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction; construction; wholesale trade; retail trade; information; financial activities; social assistance; leisure and hospitality; other services; and government.
And visually:
Since the numbers were red hot, top to bottom, it was expected that Treasuries dipped as the surge in US job growth led traders to add to wagers that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates when officials next meet in December. The declines on Friday pushed yields higher across maturities, with those on two-year notes — more sensitive to the outlook for the Fed’s rate path than longer peers — up by as much as seven basis points to 4.54%. The 10-year yield was four basis points higher at 4.87% after data showed the US added 165,000 jobs in October, topping forecasts.
Traders maintained expectations of further rate hikes from the US central bank, pricing in a 70% chance of a quarter-point rate hike next month. All told, the market expects at least 40 basis points of additional tightening by September 2027, according to Bloomberg.

WASHINGTON — The job market likely bounced back last month from a disappointing September. Layoffs are low, and most Americans enjoy unusual job security.
But hiring has probably remained too modest to deliver much relief to those looking for work. And wage gains haven't been keeping up with persistently high inflation.
Labor Department revisions added 84,000 new jobs in August and September.
The unemployment rate fell even though 421,000 people entered the labor force.
But hourly wages rose a meager 3.1% from October 2025, with many families struggling to keep up with inflation.
Professional and business services – a broad category of administrative and managerial workers – added 70,000. Healthcare companies hired nearly 42,000. Factories added 19,000 jobs. But hotels, restaurants and bars cut 10,600.
The jobs report arrives three days after voters handed a stunning defeat to President Donald Trump and his Republican Party in midterm elections. Frustrated with the state of the economy — and especially the high cost of living – Americans handed full control of Congress to the Democrats.
Yet the American economy and job market have proven resilient in the face of a series of shocks — Trump's double-digit taxes on imports and the war with Iran, which has driven gasoline prices above $4 a gallon and pinched family budgets.
Gross domestic product — the nation's output of goods and services — advanced at a sprightly 3.4% annual pace from July through September, lifted by strong consumer spending and booming investment in artificial intelligence.
The job market has been solid but unspectacular.
So far this year, employers — companies, government agencies and nonprofits — have added an average of 68,000 jobs a month, including a disappointing 29,000 last month. Last year, high interest rates and President Donald Trump's unpredictable trade policies discouraged hiring.
Despite recovering this year, hiring remains well below the average of 166,000 monthly jobs created in 2023 and 2024, let alone the 491,000 a month recorded during the 2021-2022 hiring boom that followed COVID-19 lockdowns.
