sources.text:
The United States added 165,000 jobs in October, far exceeding economists’ forecasts, as the labor market remained resilient despite the Federal Reserve’s recent interest-rate increases.
The unemployment rate edged down to 4.1%, even as labor force participation rose slightly. The September jobs report, which had initially recorded a modest gain of 29,000 jobs, was also revised upward to 60,000.
Heather Long, Chief Economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, called the results “a blowout” in a post on X.
Economists surveyed by Bloomberg forecast that employment would increase by approximately 70,000 jobs in October, while the unemployment rate would remain unchanged. Wages rose 0.4% from September, exceeding the 0.3% month-over-month increase economists had expected. Annual earnings climbed 3.1%, surpassing forecasts but likely remaining below the current inflation rate.
Employment Opportunities & Market Effects
Employers created jobs across several sectors of the economy. Professional and business services, previously considered more exposed to AI-related disruption, added 70,000 positions. Healthcare, a longstanding source of strong job growth, gained 42,000 jobs—above average. Employment in transportation and warehousing increased by 25,000, while manufacturing maintained its strength, adding 19,000 jobs.
“This is still a low-hire, low-fire market overall, but we could be seeing some green shoots on the hiring side,” Jake Krimmel, Senior Economist at Realtor.com.
Other labor market indicators released earlier this week pointed to steady hiring, though none matched Friday’s unexpectedly strong jobs report. The Labor Department’s monthly Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey showed modest increases in job openings and hiring. ADP reported that private employers added 86,000 jobs, while layoff plans fell to a three-year low and seasonal hiring accelerated.
“Consistent with prior, more partial indicators of the US labor market, the October Jobs Report came in very strong, across the board,” Wharton Economist Mohamed El-Erian posted on X.
The strong report is likely to increase the Federal Reserve’s confidence in proceeding with another interest rate hike in December. Before announcing its decision on Dec. 9, the central bank will also assess November employment data and October inflation figures. Traders now assign a 77% probability to a 25-basis-point rate increase next month, compared with 67% on Thursday, according to CME FedWatch.
“Today’s jobs report is a strong rebuttal to fears that the economy is heading into a meaningful slowdown,” Seema Shah, Chief Global Strategist at Principal Asset Management. “With wage growth also picking up, a December Fed hike remains firmly on the table despite the recent tightening in financial conditions.”
The recent acceleration in hiring has not yet reduced the time unemployed people spend looking for work after losing a job. Layoffs remain limited, and job growth has been strong enough to bring down the unemployment rate. However, people who lose their jobs are, on average, staying unemployed longer than at any point in the past five years.
Setting aside the brief spike in unemployment during the COVID-19 pandemic, the median and average durations of unemployment—11.9 weeks and 27.1 weeks, respectively—are the longest in roughly a decade. Most economists agree that the growing adoption of artificial intelligence tools by employers has not yet led to widespread job losses across the economy. However, that does not mean such losses are entirely absent.
“The most AI-exposed sectors, information and finance, continued to struggle and have shed jobs on a trend basis,” said Michael Pearce, Chief U.S. Economist at Oxford Economics. “By contrast, professional and business services, which also has high AI adoption, bucked that trend and added 70,000 jobs in October while seeing upward revisions to past months. Those gains were broad, spanning temporary help and management and technical consulting services.”

sources.text:
By Jeffrey Sparshott
Bloomberg News
(TNS)
U.S. job growth surged in October and the unemployment rate edged lower, signs of labor-market strength in an expanding economy.
Nonfarm payrolls increased 165,000 last month, topping all forecasts, after an upward revision to the prior two months, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data out Friday. The unemployment rate fell to 4.1%.
Employers across a broad range of sectors added jobs, including in professional and business services, healthcare and manufacturing. Overall private-sector payroll growth was the strongest since March.
Resilient consumer spending and strong business investment have supported demand and boosted corporate profits this year, encouraging companies to add more workers. Job growth has been uneven from month to month, but overall hiring has been strong enough to keep the unemployment rate at or below 4.5% for five years, the longest such stretch on record.
Federal Reserve officials will see one more jobs report and a full slate of inflation data before their next meeting in December. Investors expect them to raise interest rates at that gathering to counter inflation, following an increase in September and a subsequent decision to leave rates unchanged in October.
“The report was broadly strong,” said Oscar Munoz, head of U.S. economics at TD Securities. “This should allow the Fed to continue focusing on inflation and what’s happening in financial markets.”
If sustained, solid job growth “would bode well not only for the labor market, but also for consumption and for spending,” he added.
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh last week described employment conditions as “quite positive” and said the central bank was focused on prices. The yield on 2-year Treasury notes rose and the S&P 500 was higher following the release.
Healthcare and social assistance employers added about 55,000 workers to payrolls in October, the most in six months. That sector has been the biggest driver of job growth in recent years.
Spending on data centers and demand for AI-related infrastructure has supported construction and manufacturing employment this year. Friday’s report showed that nonresidential construction firms continued to add jobs, even as broader construction payrolls were weighed down by losses in residential building.
Factory headcount also saw solid gains, with computer and electronic product manufacturing firms adding the most jobs in four years.
“The economy has been growing above trend, and even as businesses place greater emphasis on productivity, technology and disciplined headcount management, they continue to hire where demand warrants it,” EY-Parthenon’s Gregory Daco and Lydia Boussour said in a note.
Employment in the information and financial activities sectors, which have seen some of the fastest rates of job loss and AI adoption this year, showed tentative signs of stabilization in October.
Goldman Sachs Group Inc. economists, in a note published this week, said “AI’s labor market impact has become increasingly visible in recent months,” with “higher adoption associated with weaker job growth and higher unemployment” across nonmanufacturing industries.
What Bloomberg Economics Says …
“October hiring was strong and broad-based, and the upward revisions show the summer slowdown was milder than first reported. With unemployment edging down and wage growth firming, the labor market is not loosening the way we had anticipated. We still expect the Fed to hold in December on tighter financial conditions, but the risk of another hike has risen.”
— Anna Wong, Andrew Sacher and Eliza Winger
The report also suggested the labor market is generating little wage pressure. Average hourly earnings advanced 3.1% from a year earlier, matching the slowest pace since 2021. On a monthly basis, however, they rose 0.4%, topping forecasts.
The wage figures highlight a key source of voter frustration in this week’s midterm elections. While the unemployment rate has been low, pay hasn’t kept up with inflation throughout most of 2026.
The participation rate—the share of the population that is working or actively looking for work—edged up to 61.9% in October, the highest since March. A broad measure of unemployment also rose as the ranks of those working part-time for economic reasons jumped to a six-month high.
Measures of long-term unemployment worsened, with the median duration of a jobless spell reaching 11.9 weeks, the longest since 2021. Labor-market turnover has been historically low for much of the last few years, which has made it difficult to find new jobs and led many to feel either locked out or stuck in place.
The payroll numbers have seen wild swings this year from month to month, with sometimes large deviations from economists’ estimates. The median forecast in Bloomberg’s survey for the October report was off by 95,000, and four other reports this year have seen misses at least as large.
Separate data out Friday showed U.S. consumer sentiment rose in early November to a three-month high.

sources.news_title: U.S. Hiring Rebounds Sharply In October, But Long-Term Unemployment Remains A Concern
sources.text:
US job growth accelerated in October and the unemployment rate fell to 4.1%, suggesting that the labor market could be strengthening after stumbling in mid-summer and keeping the Federal Reserve on track to raise interest rates in December.
The Labor Department’s closely watched employment report on Friday also showed the economy added 84,000 more jobs in August and September than previously reported. The decline in the unemployment rate from 4.2% in September was despite more people piling into the labor force, likely seeking to cushion themselves against higher living costs resulting from the conflict in the Middle East.
The better-than-expected report followed on the heels of data this week showing a rise in job openings in September, which combined with historically low layoffs has raised the specter of the labor market tightening.
“The labor market is heating up across-the-board and supports our view that the Fed will raise the policy rate again in December,” said Kathy Bostjancic, chief economist at Nationwide.
Nonfarm payrolls jumped by 165,000 jobs last month after an upwardly revised 60,000 gain in September, the Labor Department’s Bureau of Labor Statistics said. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast payrolls advancing 65,000 after a previously reported 29,000 increase in September.
Estimates ranged from 35,000 to 125,000 jobs. August’s employment gains were revised up to 186,000 from the previously estimated 133,000. Employment growth averaged 137,000 over the last three months compared to an average loss of 45,000 during the same period in 2025. Some economists were skeptical of the labor market’s newfound strength.
“Recent improvements in the employment situation largely relate to a major jump in federal government spending in the third quarter, as well as an unprecedented surge in election spending reported to be near $12 billion within a relatively short time frame of August to October,” said Brian Bethune, an economics professor at Boston College.
Last month’s broad-based increase in payrolls was led by the professional and business services industry, which added 70,000 jobs, well above the average monthly gain of 15,000 over the past 12 months. Those jobs were in professional, scientific and technical services as well as administrative and support, waste management and remediation services.
Healthcare employment increased by 42,000 jobs, mostly at hospitals and home healthcare services. The transportation and warehousing sector added 25,000 positions, the majority of them couriers and messengers, consistent with strong domestic demand.
Manufacturing payrolls rose by 19,000 jobs, spread across computer and electronic products, machinery and primary metals. The increases are likely linked to the artificial intelligence buildout. There were modest job gains in the retail, financial activities and government sectors.
Construction Loses Jobs
Construction shed 3,000 jobs, the bulk of them residential specialty trade contractors. Residential building construction employment also declined against the backdrop of high mortgage rates, which have depressed homebuilding. Home renovations have also been trending down.
Leisure and hospitality employment dropped by 13,000 positions, concentrated in the accommodation and food services sector. The share of industries reporting growth last month increased to 57.6% from 54.2% in September. The average workweek was unchanged at 34.4 hours.
Financial markets priced in a roughly 80% chance of a rate hike at the US central bank’s meeting next month, up from 66.9% on Thursday, CME’s FedWatch tool showed.
The Fed last week left its benchmark overnight interest rate in the 3.75%-4.00% range. Next Tuesday’s consumer inflation report for October could offer more clues on the course of monetary policy in early 2027. Economists are also watching the stock market after a tech-sector rout on Thursday amid fears a Democratic-led Congress could lead to tougher AI regulation.
Stocks on Wall Street were trading higher. The dollar gained versus a basket of currencies. US Treasury yields rose.
Economists estimated the economy needs to create at least 40,000 jobs per month to keep up with growth in the working-age population. The so-called breakeven rate has declined from roughly 150,000 in 2024 because of the smaller labor force as the Trump administration cracks down on immigration.
Household employment, a volatile measure, increased 463,000 in October, outpacing the 421,000 people who entered the labor force. About 1.589 million people have joined the labor force over the past three months, lifting the participation rate to 61.9% from 61.6% in August. But many of them, mostly re-entrees, have not found work.
Young adults have virtually been locked out of the labor market, with AI eliminating some entry-level positions.
The median duration of unemployment jumped to 11.9 weeks, the longest since November 2021, from 11.5 weeks in September. There were more people working part-time for economic reasons last month, with the number increasing 339,000 to 4.840 million.
A broader measure of unemployment, which includes people who want to work but have given up searching and those working part-time because they cannot find full-time employment, rose to 7.9% from 7.6% in September. Historically low layoffs have anchored the labor market.
Though hiring is picking up, it has lagged economic growth, with gross domestic product increasing at a 3.4% annualized rate in the third quarter. Economists said uncertainty from the US-Israeli war with Iran as well as the impact of AI on staffing needs had left businesses hesitant to increase head count.
“More than a quarter of unemployed workers were searching for six months or longer in October, a share rarely seen outside the aftermath of a recession,” said Cory Stahle, senior economist at the Indeed Hiring Lab. “And even when employers do hire, job posting data suggests that they have increasingly tilted their hiring toward experience, leaving people early in their careers with even fewer ways in.”
Wage growth maintained its moderate pace, increasing 3.1% in the 12 months through October after advancing 3.2% in September. While that underscored the disinflationary impulse from the labor market, it illustrated the continued erosion of household incomes. Consumer prices rose 3.7% year-on-year in September.
Anger over inflation resulted in President Donald Trump’s Republican Party losing control of Congress to Democrats in Tuesday’s midterm elections.
“The American public will continue to skeptically look at the current economic expansion which is highly skewed towards upper- end households and corporates that are profiting from strong underlying demand and robust non-residential investment,” said Joseph Brusuelas, chief economist at RSM.

Housing market may see ‘more churn’ after strong job gains 
The U.S. economy added 165,000 jobs in October, far outpacing forecasts and raising the odds of another Fed hike at the central bank’s next meeting.
The surprisingly strong October jobs data released Nov. 6 will likely raise the odds of another short-term interest rate hike when the Federal Reserve meets next month, though labor market momentum may also lead to a little more activity for the ice-cold housing market.
Job gains outpace forecasts: The U.S. economy added 165,000 jobs last month, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, smashing forecaster expectations of 59,000 added jobs in October. The unemployment rate declined a tick to 4.1%.
Despite the surge in new jobs, annual wage growth held at a relatively normal pace of 3.1%, continuing the months-long trend of inflation — which came in at 3.7% in September — outpacing this measure of growth.
But there are warning signs for construction: While the overall jobs report pointed to a stronger labor market, this was not the case for hiring in residential construction. Employment in that sector fell by 16,400 jobs in October, the biggest monthly drop since March 2021, according to the National Association of Home Builders.
Meanwhile, nonresidential construction employment rose by 13,300, a sign that data center construction held strong heading into the midterms. But investors appeared to be concerned about a potential slowdown after voters indicated they were not happy with this sector's construction boom, leading to a sell-off of tech stocks earlier this week.
Investors predicting a December rate hike: With the overall labor market seemingly in good shape, investors widely expect the Fed to focus on lowering inflation at its next meeting. As of Nov. 6, the CME Group's FedWatch tool estimated the likelihood of a short-term interest rate hike in December was around 79.1%, up from 66.9% a day earlier.
Rates still above 7% despite recent drops: After peaking at around 7.4% in mid-October, the 30-year fixed-rate mortgage has trended down over the past few weeks and is now averaging around 7.18%. While more jobs could spur additional fluctuations, the recent decline in rates is coming at what is typically the beginning of the housing market's slowest time of year.
Economy's 'major wildcard' still in play: The October jobs report delivered the type of data that cuts both ways for real estate, said Sam Williamson, senior economist at First American. "More jobs mean more income and more reasons to move, while a stronger economy could prolong the wait for mortgage-rate relief," Williamson said. "Still, a healthier labor market could put a little more churn into a housing market stuck in a low-churn, slow-burn recovery."
Despite the flashy jobs numbers, the results of the midterm elections continue to dominate discussions about what to expect in the year ahead. The jobs report was better than expected with an upward revision.
Understanding the Lead Chart
Note: If you have seen this explanation, please skip to down to the subtitle “Initial Thoughts” to continue reading.
Every January (typically), the BLS has annual revisions to nonfarm payrolls and household population employment. The BLS does not back revise the household charts.
Because the BLS does not back revise, we see ridiculous numbers such as employment rising by over 2 million in a month (first yellow arrow).
To correct for the population adjustments, the BLS provides an adjustment series to normalize employment levels to match nonfarm payrolls. The BLS calls this “experimental” data but the regular posted data is admitted nonsense.
The experimental series is LNS16000000, “Employment Adjusted to CES Concepts“.
For 2024, the BLS admits that it undercounted employment by 2 million. Instead of parsing that out in the correct months, the BLS plowed the entire adjustment into January of 2025.
For 2025, the BLS admits that it overcounted employment by 1.4 million. Instead of parsing that out in the correct months, the BLS plowed the entire adjustment into January of 2026.
We did not suddenly add 2.245 million jobs in January of 2025, all US-Born. (Difference between the dashed blue line and the yellow line).
Moreover, there is no valid historical data on full vs parttime employment, on foreign born employment, and many other BLS data series. And there won’t be. There are no back adjustments key data components.
All posts on foreign-born employment, parttime employment, etc., suffer this flaw. All year-over-year (or December-to January) analysis you find on these stats is permanently flawed.
2025 Experimental Data
In April, the BLS released Experimental series accounting for January 2026 population control effects.
(Official CPS estimates for December 2025 and earlier months have not been revised, in accordance with usual practice.)
Experimental Series
In 2025, BLS produced new experimental time series measures to account for the size and timing of the large population changes reflected in the January 2025 population control adjustment.
The experimental series use the monthly time series (back to April 2020) available from the Census Bureau’s Vintage 2025 population estimates that form the basis of the January 2026 CPS population control adjustment.
The experimental series are smoother over time, as they do not show the annual effects of the population control adjustments that occur each January in the official series.
The experimental series adjusts data back to April 2020, the decennial census reference point.
Standard vs More Accurate Experimental Data
- Between December 2024 and January 2025, the standard data shows an increase of 2,245,000. The adjusted data shows a gain of 692,000.
- For December 2025, the employment level is a reported 163,992,000 vs the adjusted data at 162,557,000.
- By December 2025, the standard data employment level was overstated by 1,365,000. That did not happen in a single month. It was the result of cumulative months of bad data every month for a full year.
By standard practice, the BLS leaves the published data and charts in a known-to-be-wrong state.
Thus, all standard year-over-year household data comparisons are nonsense. Comparisons between January and December of the prior year are also invalid.
Initial Thoughts
I will continue to use what the BLS refers to as “experimental data” because the official household data is admitted nonsense.
This was a beat the street set of numbers except for a big divergence in two measures of unemployment, discussed below.
Here are the latest, undoubtedly wrong, and soon to be revised monthly job report details.
Monthly Job Report Details
- Nonfarm Payroll: +165,000 to 159,293,000 – Establishment Survey
- Civilian Non-institutional Population: +128,000 to 275,682,000
- Civilian Labor Force: +421,000 to 170,683,000 – Household Survey
- Participation Rate: +0.1 to 61.9% – Household Survey
- Employment: +463,000 to 163,615,000 – Household Survey
- Unemployment: -41,000 to 7,068,000 – Household Survey
- Baseline Unemployment Rate: -0.1 to 4.1% – Household Survey
- Not in Labor Force: -293,000 to 104,999,000 – Household Survey
- U-6 unemployment: +0.3 to 7.9% – Household Survey
Nonfarm Payrolls Change by Sector
Nonfarm Payrolls Change by Sector in Thousands
- Nonfarm Payrolls:+165
- Manufacturing: +19
- Construction: -3
- Leisure and Hospitality: +53
- Private Education and Health Care: +20
- Professional and Business Services: +70
- Information: -1
- Financial: +7
- Retail: +6
- Wholesale: -9
- Government: +6
Government Jobs Breakdown
- State: +8
- Federal: -1
- Local: -1
That was a good, and relatively balanced set of numbers.
Monthly Revisions
- The change in total nonfarm payroll employment for August was revised up by 53,000, from +133,000 to +186,000
- The change for September was revised up by 31,000, from +29,000 to +60,000.
- With these revisions, employment in August and September combined is 84,000 higher than previously reported.
Part-Time Jobs
- Involuntary Part-Time Work: +339,000 to 4,840,000
- Voluntary Part-Time Work: -149,000 to 22,664,000
- Total Full-Time Work: +717,000 to 135,090,000
- Total Part-Time Work: -242,000 to 28,504,000
- Multiple Job Holders: -101,000 to 8,805,000
The above numbers never total correctly due to the way the BLS makes seasonal adjustments. I list them as reported.
These numbers are highly unreliable for reasons noted above. Year-over-year comparisons are invalid, period. The BLS does not update these numbers in the experimental data.
Hours and Wages
- Average weekly hours of all private employees was flat at 34.4 hours.
- Average weekly hours of all private service-providing employees was flat at 33.3 hours.
- Average weekly hours of manufacturers was flat at to 40.5 hours.
This data is only as good as the data collection.
Hourly Earnings
This data is frequently revised. Here are the numbers as reported this month.
Average Hourly Earnings of All Nonfarm Workers rose $0.14 to $38.00. A year ago the average wage was $36.85. That’s a gain of 3.1%.
Average hourly earnings of Production and Nonsupervisory Workers rose $0.12 to $32.75. A year ago the average wage was $31.70. That’s a gain of 3.3%.
Accurately counted, these gains are not close to keeping up with inflation.
By accurate counting I mean factoring in homeowner’s insurance, property taxes, and tips on food. All three are excluded from the CPI. The BLS weights on food at home vs away are also wrong.
Unemployment Rate
Alternative Measures of Unemployment
The October numbers are interesting.
While the unemployment rate fell by a tenth of a point, there was a three-tenths rise in people who are discouraged or marginally-attached workers.
Table A-15 is where one can find a better approximation of what the unemployment rate really is.
- The official unemployment rate is 4.1 percent.
- U-6 is much higher at 7.9 percent.
Both numbers would be way higher still, were it not for millions dropping out of the labor force over the past few years.
Some of those dropping out of the labor force retired because they wanted to retire. Some dropped out over Covid fears and never returned. Still others took advantage of a strong stock market and retired early.
The rest is disability fraud, forced retirement (need for Social Security income), and discouraged workers.
The entire series is flawed by non-applied annual benchmark revisions.
The series is also flawed by poor response rates, deportations, illegals not answering phones, sampling errors and non-sampling errors.
Birth Death Model
Starting January 2014, I dropped the Birth/Death Model charts from this report.
The birth-death model pertains to the birth and death of corporations not individuals except by implication.
For those who follow the numbers, I retain this caution: Do not subtract the reported Birth-Death number from the reported headline number. That approach is statistically invalid.
Birth-Death Methodology Explained
I gave a detailed explanation of the model and why the usual calculation is wrong in my June 8, 2024 post How Much Did the BLS Birth-Death Adjustment Pad the May Jobs Report?
I repeat, do not subtract the birth-death number from the headline number.
Household Survey vs. Payroll Survey
- The payroll survey (sometimes called the establishment survey) is the headline jobs number. It is based on employer reporting.
- The household survey is a phone survey conducted by the BLS. It measures employment, unemployment and other factors.
If you work one hour, you are employed. If you don’t have a job and fail to look for one, you are not considered unemployed, rather, you drop out of the labor force.
Foreign-Born Employment
The numbers in my charts are seasonally adjusted. Foreign born employment is not adjusted, compounding comparison errors.
And we have no BLS revised data for foreign born employment. So, all such foreign and US-born comparisons with BLS data remain nonsense.
A second major problem with foreign-born employment is the BLS makes no distinction between US citizens who were foreign born and genuine foreign workers.
Comments on BLS Data
The BLS monthly data is garbage.I do the best with BLS data that I can, or anyone can.
The quarterly QCEW and Business Employment (BED)reports represent a 96 percent sample. But those reports lag by about 5 months.
The Birth-Death model that feeds the monthly jobs report is bogus. It has been screwed up since Covid, first underreporting jobs then overreporting them.
QCEW and BED data show more jobs are now being lost in closing businesses than gained in new businesses.
Annual revisions have been lower for three consecutive years.
However, there are hints from QCEW that the bulk of negative annual revisions may finally be in the past.
Final Thoughts – Do I Believe These Numbers?
In one word no, at least the Household numbers. The economy did not add 717,000 full-time workers.

Are illegal immigrants answering these surveys? If not, then other individuals are overweighted.
A decline in the unemployment rate coupled with a much bigger rise in the U-6 unemployment rate also adds to the mistrust.
The establishment data is also suspect, but less so. Are minority firms or firms dependent on immigrants answering these surveys?
If not, then survey responses from firms not dependent on immigrants are overweight, boosting the numbers.

WASHINGTON, D.C. — The U.S. economy added 165,000 jobs in October, while the unemployment rate remained relatively steady at 4.1%, according to a report released Friday, November 6, by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.
The October employment increase exceeded the average monthly gain of 48,000 jobs recorded over the previous 12 months. The unemployment rate edged down from 4.2% in September, with approximately 7.1 million people unemployed nationwide.
October Employment Report at a Glance
Employment Gains by Industry
Professional and business services recorded the largest reported increase among the highlighted industries, adding 70,000 jobs in October. The sector’s average monthly increase over the previous year was 15,000 jobs.
Healthcare added 42,000 positions, including gains in hospitals, home healthcare services and outpatient care centers.
Transportation and warehousing employment increased by 25,000 jobs, primarily reflecting additional hiring among couriers and messengers. Manufacturing employment also continued to rise, adding 19,000 jobs.
| Industry | Jobs Added | 
|---|---|
| Professional and Business Services | 70,000 | 
| Healthcare | 42,000 | 
| Transportation and Warehousing | 25,000 | 
| Manufacturing | 19,000 | 
Wages and Labor Force Participation
Average hourly earnings for employees on private nonfarm payrolls increased by 14 cents, or 0.4%, to $38.00 in October. Over the previous 12 months, average hourly earnings increased by 3.1%.
The labor force participation rate remained relatively unchanged at 61.9%, while the employment-population ratio was 59.3%.
The number of people working part time for economic reasons increased by 339,000 to 4.8 million. This category includes individuals who would prefer full-time employment but are working reduced hours or have been unable to find full-time positions.
Long-Term Unemployment and Revised Figures
Approximately 2 million people had been unemployed for 27 weeks or longer, accounting for 27.6% of all unemployed individuals. That figure changed little from September.
The Labor Department also revised employment figures for the previous two months. August job growth was revised upward from 133,000 to 186,000, while September’s increase was revised from 29,000 to 60,000.
Combined, the revisions show 84,000 more jobs were added during August and September than previously reported.

U.S. Employers Add 165,000 Jobs in October in Surprisingly Strong Report
Dow Jones predicted only 59,000 added jobs, and September totals were revised up by 31,000 jobs
By Brian Pascus November 6, 2026 11:19 am
reprints
The nation’s job growth had been sparse, but then came an October surprise.
The U.S. added an impressive 165,000 jobs in October, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The metric is a major increase from the 29,000 jobs that had been added in September, a number later revised to 60,000 jobs, and light years ahead of the 59,000 non-farm payroll jobs Dow Jones had forecasted as early as Friday morning.
Moreover, the U.S. unemployment rate ticked down to 4.1 percent. At 189,000 jobless claims, layoffs now sit near the historic lows of 1969.
The new numbers also provide clarity to the Federal Reserve, which has a dual mandate to fight inflation and keep unemployment low. With joblessness relatively under control, the Fed can devote its attention to taming inflation, which continues to bedevil an economy encountering headwinds from oil spikes, tariffs and stubborn price increases.
Last week, in a 10-2 vote, the Federal Reserve’s Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) kept its benchmark interest rate between 3.75 percent and 4 percent, even though inflation remains well above the central bank’s 2 percent target.
The Fed is likely to hike interest rates at least once before the year is out, per analyses of comments made by chairman Kevin Warsh.
But the news from October has offered some respite to a shaky economy. Professional and business services added 70,000 jobs last month, health care added 42,000, while the financial sector added 7,000 jobs, according to BLS data.
That said, the jobs picture has been muddled for quite some time.
Payroll growth from January 2025 through September 2026 averaged just 35,000 jobs, and there has only been once in that time when more than 200,000 jobs were added in a single month, while seven months saw net job losses, according to CNBC.

sources.text:
The US jobs October report was far stronger than expected. The economy added 165,000 jobs last month, against a consensus of 65,000 in an LSEG poll, and the unemployment rate fell to 4.1%, Fox Business reported on 6 November 2026.
The data raised expectations that the Federal Reserve will lift interest rates again at its 8 to 9 December meeting. CME FedWatch put the chance of a quarter-point rise at 76.8% after the release, Finwire reported.
Key Takeaways
- Nonfarm payrolls rose 165,000 in October, against estimates ranging from 59,000 to about 70,000.
- Unemployment fell to 4.1% from 4.2%.
- August and September were revised up by a combined 84,000 jobs.
- Average hourly earnings rose 0.4% on the month and 3.1% on the year.
- December hike odds rose to between 73% and 77% on CME FedWatch, depending on the reading.
US Jobs October: The Headline Numbers
According to Fox Business and Finwire:
- Payrolls: +165,000 in October, against a 12-month average of 48,000.
- Unemployment rate: 4.1%, below the 4.2% expected.
- August: revised up 53,000 to 186,000.
- September: revised up 31,000 to 60,000, from an initial 29,000.
Forecasts varied by survey. LSEG’s poll expected 65,000, a Dow Jones survey 59,000 and a Bloomberg survey about 70,000, according to Fox Business, Finwire and Yahoo Finance. By any measure, the US jobs October figure was more than double expectations.
Labour force participation rose slightly, Yahoo Finance said.
Where the US Jobs October Gains Came From
Services led the way. According to Finwire:
Professional and business services: +70,000
This compared with a 12-month average of 15,000. Professional, scientific and technical services added 33,000, administrative and support services 28,000, and management of companies 9,000. The sector is up 269,000 since its October 2025 low.
Healthcare: +42,000
This was above the 12-month average of 31,000.
Transportation and warehousing: +25,000
This included 17,000 couriers and messengers and 4,000 in air transportation.
Manufacturing: +19,000
Yahoo Finance reported a 19,000 gain in manufacturing. Mortgage Professional America said residential construction lost more than 15,000 jobs.
US Jobs October: Wages and Underemployment
Average hourly earnings rose 0.4% in October, against an expected 0.3%, and 3.1% over 12 months, against an expected 2.9%, Finwire reported.
Yahoo Finance noted that annual wage growth was likely still below the current inflation rate. US consumer prices rose 3.7% in the 12 months to September, according to the Bureau of Labour Statistics.
The broader U-6 underemployment rate rose to 7.9% from 7.6%, Mortgage Professional America reported. The Mortgage Bankers Association’s Mike Fratantoni said that suggests weaker underemployment conditions than the headline rate implies.
What Economists Said About the US Jobs October Data
Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, called the US jobs October numbers “a blowout” in a post on X, Yahoo Finance reported.
“Today’s jobs report is a strong rebuttal to fears that the economy is heading into a meaningful slowdown,” said Seema Shah of Principal Asset Management, according to Mortgage Professional America.
Economist Mohamed El-Erian wrote that the report “came in very strong,” consistent with earlier partial indicators of the labour market, Yahoo Finance said.
December Rate Hike Bets Grow
The US jobs report for October strengthened expectations of a Fed rate rise. Readings of CME FedWatch after the release included:
- 76.8% for a quarter-point hike in December, Finwire.
- About 77%, Mortgage Professional America.
- 73%, up from 67% on Thursday, Yahoo Finance.
The Fed held its target range at 3.75% to 4% on 28 October, after raising rates in September. The US economy grew at a 3.4% annualised rate in the third quarter, Finwire said.
St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem said on Friday that “people are still concerned about the current level of inflation,” according to Bloomingbit. On 30 October, he said further tightening would be “necessary, and soon.”
The Fed will also weigh October inflation and November jobs data before its 9 December decision, Yahoo Finance noted. We make no forecast for US interest rates.
Market Reaction to the US Jobs October Data
Treasury yields rose after the report. The 10-year yield reached 4.9%, and the 2-year moved above 4.5%, MoneyCheck reported.
Stocks were mixed. The Nasdaq rose about 1.1% in early trading as chip stocks recovered from Thursday’s sell-off, while the Dow fell, Dimsum Daily reported.
For earlier coverage of how jobs data move markets, see our reports on Asian markets after a strong US jobs report and the dollar falling as jobs were revised lower.
US Jobs October vs Alternative Data
The official figure was far above private estimates. Revelio Labs’ Public Labour Statistics, published on 5 November, estimated only about 26,000 jobs added in October, according to a Revelio Labs release.
US Jobs October FAQ
How many jobs did the US add in October 2026? 165,000, against forecasts of between 59,000 and about 70,000, with unemployment falling to 4.1%.
Which sectors added the most jobs? Professional and business services (+70,000), healthcare (+42,000) and transportation and warehousing (+25,000), Finwire reported.
What does it mean for the Fed? CME FedWatch odds of a December hike rose to between 73% and 77% after the report.
Final Thoughts
The US jobs October report showed a labour market far stronger than forecasters expected, with upward revisions to earlier months and faster wage growth. That adds to the case Fed hawks have been making for another rate rise.
October inflation data, due in mid-November, are the next test before the Fed’s December meeting.

sources.news_title: US Job Growth Smashes Forecasts With 165000 Added
sources.text:
US job growth smashes forecasts with 165000 added
The United States labor market delivered a stunningly strong performance in October 2026, adding 165,000 nonfarm payroll jobs in a powerful rebuttal to fears of an economic slowdown. Data released on November 6, 2026, by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) also showed the unemployment rate ticking down to 4.1%.
These figures blew past economists’ consensus estimates, which had predicted a far more modest gain of around 65,000 jobs and an unemployment rate of 4.2%. The robust report complicates the Federal Reserve’s upcoming decision on interest rates, as the central bank continues its fight against inflation.
Job growth smashes slowdown narrative
It also comes after a volatile period for investors, with some hedge funds hit hard by the recent October market rout.
Hiring proved surprisingly widespread across multiple industries, a departure from recent trends where healthcare often dominated growth. Professional and business services led all sectors, adding a robust 70,000 positions. This included significant gains with professional, scientific, and technical services contributing 33,000 jobs, and consulting adding 17,000 roles.
Healthcare continued its steady expansion, tallying an additional 42,000 jobs, with hospitals accounting for 16,000 of that total. Home health care services added 11,000 jobs, while outpatient care centers increased by 5,000. Transportation and warehousing grew by 25,000, and the manufacturing sector added 19,000 jobs, signaling continued demand for durable goods.
“The overall picture is a labor market that is on much better footing than a year ago,” said Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union. She noted that in 2025, the economy averaged barely 10,000 jobs a month, almost all in one sector. “This year hiring is averaging nearly 75,000 a month and there’s a much more broad based range of opportunities.”
Adding to the positive sentiment, the BLS issued substantial upward revisions to previous months’ data. The August figure was revised up by 53,000 to 186,000. September’s count also saw an increase, boosted by 31,000 to 60,000. Combined, employment over those two months was 84,000 higher than first reported.
Federal Reserve faces renewed pressure on rates
This unexpectedly strong jobs report lands at a pivotal moment for the Federal Reserve. Central bankers are weighing whether to implement another interest rate hike at their next meeting on December 8-9. Persistent strength in hiring, coupled with rising wages, puts more pressure on policymakers to continue their tightening cycle to cool demand.
Following the report’s release, traders in the futures market increased the implied probability of a quarter-percentage-point rate hike in December to 76.8%, according to the CME Group’s FedWatch tool. A tight labor market empowers workers to demand higher pay, which can fuel consumer spending and keep inflation stubbornly above the Fed’s 2% target.
The economic data also carries political weight, arriving just after a major election where household affordability was a central theme for voters. The new congressional leadership, under Democratic control, has campaigned heavily on addressing these cost-of-living issues. Such discussions around economic regulation could become more prominent, especially after recent policy shifts.
For now, the report acts as “a strong rebuttal to fears that the economy is heading into a meaningful slowdown,” according to Seema Shah, chief global strategist at Principal Asset Management. It suggests the economy is absorbing tighter financial conditions more comfortably than many had anticipated, defying earlier predictions.
Digging deeper into the labor force data
Beyond the headline numbers, the report offered a mixed but mostly positive view of the American workforce. The overall labor force participation rate, which measures the share of the population either working or looking for work, held steady at 61.9%. The employment-population ratio was also little changed at 59.3%.
Encouragingly, the civilian labor force itself expanded by 421,000 people in October. This reverses a previous trend of a shrinking workforce, which had been attributed to demographic changes and immigration reductions. At the same time, the household survey, a separate measure from the payrolls data, found that 463,000 more people reported being employed.
But not all indicators were positive. The number of people employed part-time for economic reasons—meaning they would prefer full-time work but cannot find it—increased by 339,000 to 4.8 million. This suggests some underlying slack or mismatch in the market despite the strong hiring figures, highlighting ongoing challenges for certain workers.
A worrying rise in long-term unemployment
Perhaps the most concerning detail in the October report was a sharp spike in long-term unemployment. The average duration of joblessness jumped by 2.3 weeks to 27.1 weeks, the highest it has been since September 2021. This indicates that while many people are finding work, those remaining unemployed are staying jobless for a significantly longer time.
The number of people out of work for 27 weeks or more rose to 2.0 million. This group now accounts for 27.6% of all unemployed people in the country. It points to a growing challenge where a segment of the labor force risks becoming detached, even as companies are broadly hiring across many sectors.
What the wage growth numbers really mean
For American workers, the report brought welcome news on pay. Average hourly earnings for all private-sector employees rose by 14 cents to $38.00. That’s a 0.4% increase for the month and a 3.1% increase over the past 12 months, both figures beating economists’ expectations for 0.3% and 2.9% respectively.
This sustained wage growth reflects a competitive labor market where businesses must offer higher pay to attract and retain talent. This trend was also highlighted in the recent ADP private payrolls report, whose chief economist noted that job-changers were being lured by bonuses and more hours in addition to higher base pay.
However, what’s good for a worker’s wallet is a concern for the Federal Reserve. Officials watch wage growth closely as a key driver of inflation. If wages rise too quickly, companies may pass those increased labor costs on to consumers through higher prices, creating a difficult cycle to break.
The current 3.1% annual wage growth is still well above the level consistent with the Fed’s 2% inflation target. This will almost certainly be a central topic of discussion at the upcoming December policy meeting and reinforces the case for those officials arguing for higher rates for longer.
Outlook for the coming months
Looking ahead, the U.S. labor market appears to be on solid ground but is sending some conflicting signals. The robust job creation and upward revisions to prior months paint a picture of an economy with significant momentum. It has largely defied predictions of a slowdown and continues to generate opportunities for workers.
Yet, the concerning rise in long-term unemployment and the number of involuntary part-time workers suggests the recovery is not reaching everyone equally. Cracks are appearing within the market, even if the overall foundation remains strong for now. The coming holiday season will be a key test of consumer and business confidence.
The immediate focus now shifts squarely to the Federal Reserve’s meeting on December 8-9. This jobs report gives policymakers clear justification to raise interest rates again if they choose to prioritize the inflation fight above all else.
The central bank must now weigh the risk of doing too much and tipping a resilient economy into a recession against the risk of doing too little and letting inflation become entrenched.

Inflation is overtaking unemployment as the top priority for the Federal Reserve in light of a stronger-than-expected October jobs report.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics released its monthly report on Friday morning, showing an uptick of 165,000 jobs last month dropping the unemployment rate from 4.2% to 4.1%.

The report is the first major economic indicator released since last week's Federal Open Market Committee meeting, at which the group opted to hold interest rates steady between 3.75% and 4%.
The BLS report alone does little to change the Fed's outlook on the economy, which for months has been squarely focused on persistently high inflation rather than the health of the labor market.
"The jobless rate is lower than a year ago, and payroll growth is noticeably above last year's pace," Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said during his post FOMC press conference last week. "The four-week moving average of unemployment insurance claims continues to run at the lowest level in generations. sources.news_title: US Economy Adds 165,000 Jobs as December Fed Rate Hike Odds Rise
sources.text:
Friday’s Bureau of Labor Statistics report exceeded forecasts of approximately 70,000 new jobs. The unemployment rate declined from 4.2% in September, while labor force participation increased to 61.9%, suggesting the improvement was not simply driven by workers leaving the labor market.
Interest rate futures indicated approximately a 73% probability of a 25-basis-point increase at the Federal Reserve’s December meeting, compared with around 67% on Thursday, according to CME FedWatch data cited following the release.
The report strengthens the argument that the Fed can continue addressing elevated inflation without immediately threatening employment, although officials still have additional economic data to consider before their December 9 decision.
How Broad Was October’s Employment Recovery?
October’s payroll increase represents a substantial improvement from September, when the economy initially reported just 29,000 new jobs. That figure was subsequently revised upward to 60,000.
Revisions to August and September added a combined 84,000 jobs, making the labor market stronger than previously estimated. The latest reading also exceeded the average monthly increase of approximately 48,000 recorded over the preceding 12 months.
The recovery contrasts with September’s unexpectedly weak employment report, which had temporarily reduced expectations for further Federal Reserve tightening.
Professional and business services led October’s gains, adding 70,000 positions. Healthcare contributed another 42,000 jobs, while transportation and warehousing added 25,000. Manufacturing employment increased by 19,000.
However, the gains were concentrated in several industries rather than evenly distributed across the economy. This matters because strength in a handful of sectors does not necessarily indicate that hiring conditions have improved for workers throughout the labor market.
Labor supply has also changed. Slower workforce growth, partly associated with demographic trends and reduced immigration, means the economy may need fewer new positions each month to maintain a stable unemployment rate.
Investor Takeaway
Stronger payrolls and upward revisions reduce immediate recession concerns, giving the Fed more flexibility to maintain restrictive monetary policy.
Why Does Wage Growth Complicate the Inflation Outlook?
Average hourly earnings increased 0.4% from September, exceeding expectations for a 0.3% rise. Annual wage growth reached 3.1%, also above economists’ forecasts of 2.9%.
While stronger employment and wages support household income and consumption, they also complicate the Federal Reserve’s efforts to return inflation to its 2% target.
September’s consumer inflation rate reached 3.7%, driven partly by higher gasoline prices. The latest annual wage growth figure remains below that inflation reading, indicating continued pressure on household purchasing power.
Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh has recently argued that labor market conditions remain positive, while inflation represents the more pressing concern for policymakers.
Following the October monetary policy meeting, Warsh pointed to stronger payroll growth, historically low unemployment insurance claims and resilient economic activity as evidence that the employment side of the Fed’s dual mandate remains relatively healthy.
However, stronger hiring does not automatically mean faster inflation. Productivity improvements and changes in labor supply can allow employment to expand without producing equivalent increases in price pressures.
The October report therefore strengthens the Fed’s ability to concentrate on inflation, rather than establishing that labor market conditions are themselves generating additional price increases.
Does the Jobs Report Make a December Rate Hike Likely?
The Federal Reserve left its benchmark interest rate unchanged at 3.75%–4.00% on October 28, following a 25-basis-point increase in September. The decision passed by a 10–2 vote, with Governors Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack supporting another quarter-point increase.
The accompanying policy statement acknowledged that inflation remained elevated, even as economic activity continued expanding at a strong pace.
Before the meeting, a Reuters survey of 100 economists found unanimous expectations for a December rate increase, despite overwhelming expectations that policymakers would leave rates unchanged in October.
Friday’s employment figures reinforce that outlook, but a December increase is not guaranteed. The Fed will receive October inflation figures and another employment report before its December 8–9 meeting.
Markets reacted to the employment surprise with higher Treasury yields and a stronger dollar, reflecting expectations that interest rates could remain elevated for longer.
Higher yields can support the dollar while increasing borrowing costs and placing pressure on interest-rate-sensitive assets, including growth stocks and longer-duration bonds. However, market reactions also depend on whether investors interpret the employment strength as evidence of economic resilience or a reason for additional monetary tightening.

sources.text:
Strong Jobs Report Threatens Mortgage Rate Rally
October hiring more than doubled expectations, pushing Treasury yields higher
Mortgage professionals hoping the recent rate rally had more room to run got some unwelcome news Friday.
U.S. employers added 165,000 jobs in October, well above the 65,000 economists expected, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The unemployment rate slipped to 4.1% from 4.2%.
Bond traders reacted quickly. Treasury yields climbed following the report, putting pressure on a rally that had helped bring mortgage rates down for three consecutive weeks.
For LOs, the immediate concern is whether that shift will translate into higher borrowing costs for customers who have been holding out for better pricing.
A Rate Rally Meets Resistance
The jobs report arrived just as mortgage rates were showing some improvement.
The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate fell to 7.18% this week from 7.24% a week earlier, according to Freddie Mac. The 10-year Treasury yield had also retreated to around 4.84% Thursday, its lowest level since early September.
Friday's employment numbers interrupted that momentum.
The government revised August and September payrolls upward by a combined 84,000 jobs. Average hourly earnings rose 0.4% in October and 3.1% over the past year.
The stronger labor market also increased expectations that the Federal Reserve could raise interest rates at its December meeting. Market-implied odds of a quarter-point increase climbed to approximately 78% from 70% before the report, according to Reuters.
Sam Williamson, senior economist at First American, said the stronger hiring numbers give the Fed more room to focus on inflation.
“With hiring stronger and unemployment still low, the Federal Reserve has more room to keep its focus on inflation. The combination of solid job growth and firmer wage gains keeps a December rate hike firmly in play, though the outlook beyond December will depend on what happens with inflation and the next jobs report,” Williamson said.
Treasury yields moved higher following the release, with the benchmark 10-year yield rising to around 4.87% in early trading.
Lower Rates Haven't Brought Buyers Back
Even before Friday's report, the recent improvement in rates had done little to revive demand.
Applications fell 1.2% last week, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association, while purchase applications declined 2%. Adjustable-rate mortgages accounted for 11.4% of applications, their highest share since September 2025.
The housing market is showing similar weakness. As NMP reported Thursday, pending home sales fell 16.4% year over year despite easing home prices and mortgage payments.
That leaves originators facing a difficult combination: borrowers remain reluctant to commit even when rates improve, and Friday's jobs report could make further rate relief harder to come by.
What It Means
The immediate concern is lender pricing, particularly for borrowers with floating rates.
Mortgage rates are influenced by Treasury yields and mortgage-backed securities prices, although lender rate sheets do not necessarily move in lockstep with either market.
For purchase borrowers already stretching to qualify, a pricing reversal could affect monthly payments, discount points, or available loan options. Refinance prospects are especially sensitive to rate changes because even a modest increase can reduce potential savings.
The latest jobs figures also add another consideration for lenders planning production through year-end.
As NMP reported following the Fed's October meeting, mortgage pricing remains sensitive to bond-market movements even when the central bank leaves its benchmark rate unchanged.
Stronger employment could also give the sluggish purchase market a lift, even if mortgage rates remain elevated.
“For housing, stronger hiring cuts both ways. More jobs mean more income and more reasons to move, while a stronger economy could prolong the wait for mortgage-rate relief,” Williamson said.
For originators, that leaves a mixed picture heading into year-end. A healthier job market could bring more prospective buyers into the market, but higher borrowing costs may still keep some of them on the sidelines.
Friday's report has made the recent rate rally a little less comfortable.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics summed up its own release in one sentence: “Total nonfarm payroll employment rose by 165,000 in October, and the unemployment rate changed little at 4.1 percent.”

The October gain is the strongest headline number in this report, but the revisions change the story behind it. September first looked like a near stall at 29,000 jobs.

That combination matters for housing. Demand is being held back by the cost of borrowing, not by a collapse in employment.
Where the Jobs Came From, and the Two Numbers Most Readers Will Miss
Professional and business services increased by 70,000 in October, well above the average monthly gain of 15,000 over the prior 12 months. Within that total, professional, scientific, and technical services added 33,000, administrative and support and waste management and remediation services added 28,000, and management of companies and enterprises added 9,000.
The rest of the gains were concentrated in a few industries:
- Health care: up 42,000, above its prior 12-month average of 31,000, with hospitals up 16,000, home health care services up 11,000, and outpatient care centers up 5,000.
- Transportation and warehousing: up 25,000, reflecting growth in couriers and messengers, up 17,000, and air transportation, up 4,000.
- Manufacturing: up 19,000, and up 101,000 since a recent low in December 2025.
The first number most readers will miss is construction. Employment showed little change over the month in construction, and also in mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction, wholesale trade, retail trade, information, financial activities, social assistance, leisure and hospitality, other services, and government.
That means this was not a building-led jobs surge. It lines up with D.R. Horton’s fiscal fourth quarter, where net sales orders fell 7 percent and the cancellation rate rose to 23 percent. Hiring strength and new-home demand are moving in different directions right now.
The second missed number is part-time work. The number of people employed part time for economic reasons increased by 339,000 to 4.8 million in October.
These are people who would have preferred full-time employment but were working part time because their hours had been reduced or they were unable to find full-time jobs. The long-term unemployed, those jobless for 27 weeks or more, changed little at 2.0 million and accounted for 27.6 percent of all unemployed people.

Use this report in four practical ways:
- Underwrite rent on local jobs, not the national headline. Check whether your market is adding health care, logistics, or professional services jobs, because those were the three engines in October.
- Do not count on a construction boom to rescue supply or raise your property’s value. Construction employment showed little change, so treat new supply as a local permit question, not a national trend.
- Stress-test the part-time number. A jump of 339,000 people working part time for economic reasons is a reason to keep reserves and screen tenants on current income, not last year’s pay.
- Watch the next two dates before locking a plan: the Employment Situation for November 2026 is scheduled for Friday, December 4, 2026, at 8:30 a.m. (ET), according to the release.

October Jobs Report: U.S. Adds 165,000 Jobs

The U.S. labor market delivered a stronger-than-expected performance in October, adding 165,000 jobs and easing concerns about a prolonged hiring slowdown. The surprisingly strong employment report suggests the American economy remains resilient, although it also raises questions about the Federal Reserve’s next move on interest rates.
According to data released Friday by the Bureau of Labor Statistics, nonfarm payrolls increased by 165,000 in October, significantly exceeding economists’ expectations of approximately 65,000 jobs. The unemployment rate edged down from 4.2% in September to 4.1%, reinforcing signs of stability in the labor market.
The report represents a notable improvement from September, when employers added a revised 60,000 jobs. August’s employment figures were also revised higher, from 133,000 to 186,000, bringing the combined upward revisions for the previous two months to 84,000 jobs.
Hiring was particularly strong across professional and business services, healthcare, and transportation, suggesting that employment growth is extending into several important areas of the economy.
Professional and business services led the gains, adding 70,000 jobs during October. Healthcare and social assistance contributed approximately 55,100 positions, while transportation and warehousing added another 24,800 jobs.
Manufacturing also showed encouraging signs, adding 19,000 jobs, including gains in computer and electronic products, fabricated metals, and motor vehicles. The improvement could provide a positive signal for industrial companies and businesses supplying equipment and components to manufacturers.
However, the labor market remains uneven. Leisure and hospitality lost approximately 13,000 jobs, while wholesale trade employment declined by 9,100, demonstrating that not every sector is experiencing the same momentum.
Wage growth remained another important component of the report.
Average hourly earnings increased 0.4% in October to $38.00, representing a 3.1% increase over the past year. While higher wages support household purchasing power, continued wage growth could complicate efforts to bring inflation sustainably toward the Federal Reserve’s 2% target.
For investors, the stronger employment figures present both opportunities and challenges.
A resilient labor market can support consumer spending, business investment, and corporate earnings. Companies across retail, manufacturing, healthcare, and transportation may benefit if employment growth translates into sustained demand for goods and services.
Small-cap companies, many of which depend heavily on domestic economic activity, could be particularly sensitive to these developments.
A stronger economy can create opportunities for smaller businesses to expand operations, attract customers, and improve revenue growth. However, the interest-rate outlook remains an important consideration.
The Federal Reserve must balance supporting employment with maintaining price stability. Stronger hiring and wage growth could reduce the urgency for additional interest-rate cuts, potentially keeping borrowing costs elevated for longer.
That environment can be challenging for smaller companies that rely on bank loans or variable-rate financing to fund expansion.
For investors evaluating small-cap and microcap opportunities, companies with manageable debt, improving cash flow, and sustainable revenue growth may be better positioned to benefit from economic resilience while navigating higher financing costs.
The October report also follows Wednesday’s ADP employment data, which showed private employers adding 86,000 jobs, providing another indication that hiring conditions may be stabilizing after a period of slower growth.
Despite the encouraging headline numbers, the labor market has not returned to the rapid hiring pace experienced earlier in the economic expansion. Employers continue to approach staffing decisions cautiously, and employment gains remain concentrated in selected industries.
Nevertheless, October’s results suggest the U.S. economy entered the final quarter of 2026 on firmer footing than many economists anticipated.
For Wall Street, attention now turns to upcoming inflation data and Federal Reserve commentary, which could help determine whether stronger economic growth will support a broader market rally or delay the interest-rate relief many investors have been anticipating.
